Donald J. Trump

An Investigative Biography

From Queens to the Second Term

A Meechie's World Inc publication · Current through September 2026

About this edition

This book is a critical biography written from the public record: court filings, government reports, tax returns released by Congress, contemporaneous news reporting, and the public statements of the people it describes. Where a claim is disputed, the dispute is stated. Where Trump or his representatives have denied an allegation, the denial is recorded. The penultimate chapter presents the case for the defense.

The last chapters cover events through late September 2026 and are provisional. Court cases, wars and policies described there may have changed since.

Chapter 1
The Man in the Glass Tower

A Note Before We Begin

This is a critical, investigative biography of Donald John Trump. That word, critical, describes the method of the book and not merely its mood. The chapters that follow set out the case that his critics make, using the documentary record wherever it exists: court filings, jury verdicts, government reports, financial disclosures, contemporaneous reporting, and the public statements of Trump himself. Where a fact is contested, the book says so. Where Trump or his representatives have denied an allegation, the denial is stated. Where a claim rests on a single anonymous source, the reader is told. And because a case is only as good as its ability to withstand an answer, the penultimate chapter presents, as forcefully as its defenders would, the argument on the other side.

Readers who admire Trump will find much here that they dispute. Readers who despise him may find that some of what they believe is not supported by the record, or is more complicated than they thought. Both outcomes are acceptable to the author. The purpose of a biography of a president, above all a president who has held office twice and who has reshaped the country's politics for more than a decade, is to understand how he got here, what he did with the power he gathered, and what the record shows.

A word about currency. This book was completed at the end of September 2026. Trump is a sitting president. Many of the cases, policies and controversies described in the later chapters are unresolved, and some may have moved by the time you read this. The most recent chapters draw on news reporting and court records available in the weeks before publication. They are a snapshot, not a verdict.

The Building

Fifth Avenue between 56th and 57th Streets is one of the most expensive pieces of retail geography on earth. In 1983 a sixty-eight-story tower of bronze-tinted glass opened there, and its owner put his name on it in tall brass letters. Trump Tower was not the largest building in Manhattan, nor the most beautiful, nor even the most profitable. It was the most effective. It made a twenty-year-old idea concrete: that a name, applied to a building and repeated often enough, could be worth more than the building.

Inside, an atrium of pink Breccia Perniciano marble rose around a five-story waterfall. Above the shops and offices were apartments, and at the top a triplex penthouse decorated in a style that its owner described, with evident sincerity, as luxurious. Visitors and, later, television crews, saw gilt, mirrors, marble and gold plating. What they saw was not subtle, and it was not meant to be. It was a set for a performance about wealth, and the performance would run for four decades.

That performance is the subject of this book. The man who built the tower was thirty-seven years old when it opened. He was already a public figure, already in the gossip columns, already skilled at the trade of making journalists want to write about him. He was also, by the standards of the real estate business, a beginner, carried by his father's guarantees, by public subsidies, and by bankers who did not yet fully understand how much of his fortune was borrowed.

Within a generation he would become a television star, then a candidate, then the forty-fifth president of the United States, then a defeated incumbent who refused to concede, then a defendant in four criminal cases, then the first person convicted of felonies to be elected president, and finally the forty-seventh president. No novelist would have dared to plot it.

The Puzzle

The central problem of writing about Trump is that almost everyone who encounters him ends up telling a story about himself. To his supporters he is the one figure who was willing to say what politicians would not, to fight back against institutions they believe treated them with contempt, and to keep promises that others made and abandoned. To his opponents he is a threat to the rule of law, a serial liar, and a man whose personal appetites and grievances have been placed above the public interest.

Both portraits capture something true. Neither explains the phenomenon. Trump has been on the American stage since the late 1970s. He has won two presidential elections and lost one, has been acquitted twice by the Senate, has been indicted four times, and has seen his approval rating settle, through most of two terms, in a narrow band that rarely rose above the mid-forties. In September 2026, polling averages put his approval near thirty-six percent, among the lowest recorded for a president at this stage of a term, and yet a substantial and durable base of voters remained loyal to him. Any account that cannot explain both his strengths and his liabilities is incomplete.

This book tries to keep a few questions in view throughout.

First, how did a man who was rescued from financial disaster in the early 1990s by a coalition of banks that judged it cheaper to keep him solvent than to foreclose come to be seen as a genius of business? How much of the reputation was earned, and how much was manufactured?

Second, what is the relationship between Trump the businessman, Trump the television star, and Trump the politician? Are they one man, using one set of tools, or three?

Third, what are the patterns in his conduct: toward the truth, toward the law, toward rivals, toward the press, toward the institutions of government? Are these the patterns of an unusually forceful executive, or of something more troubling?

Fourth, what has the country actually gained and lost during the periods when he held power?

The Method of the Book

The chapters run mostly in order. The first part follows Trump from his birth in Queens in 1946 through the reinvention of his image in the 1990s and 2000s, and pauses to look at his marriages and children. The second follows him into politics: the 2016 campaign, the first term, the two impeachments, and the defeat of 2020, with chapters on his foreign policy, his language and his handling of the press, and the charges of racism that have followed him. The third concerns the crisis that followed, the events of January 6, 2021, the legal reckoning, the courts, and the remaking of the Republican Party. The fourth covers the comeback and the second term, his business dealings, and his age. The last two chapters step back, first to state the best case for the defense and then to assess what the record supports. Appendices contain a timeline, a list of principal figures and a note on sources.

The sources are of several kinds. The most reliable are documents: judgments, transcripts, tax returns released by Congress, reports by inspectors general and special counsels, and books of record such as the Federal Register. Next come investigative reports by news organizations that named their sources and showed their work. Memoirs and insider books are used with care, because their authors have their own interests. Trump's own words, as recorded in speeches, interviews, books, and social media posts, are treated as primary evidence of what he said, though not of whether it was true.

A final note on tone. Investigative writing has a temptation to condemn in adjectives. The author has tried to resist it. Facts, dates and figures do more work than epithets, and the reader is more than capable of forming a judgment.

The Shape of a Life

Donald Trump was born on June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York, the fourth of five children of Fred and Mary Anne Trump. His father was a builder of middle-class apartment complexes in the outer boroughs who had become very rich by working closely with government housing programs. His mother was a Scottish immigrant who had come to America as a domestic servant. He grew up in a large house in Jamaica Estates, attended a private day school, was sent to military school at thirteen after acts of misbehavior, studied at Fordham and then at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, and joined his father's business in 1968.

By the mid-1970s he had moved to Manhattan and begun making deals of his own. The story of what he did next, and what his father did to help him, is one of the great American business narratives, and one of the most contested. The chapters that follow examine it in detail, and they begin, appropriately, where he began: in Queens, in the shadow of a father who valued toughness above all other qualities, and who trained his son to see the world as a place where you either win or are made a fool of.

There is one more thing to say at the outset. Trump has always understood, better than most people who have sought public office, that attention is a form of power. He has never been boring. He has never been out of the news for long. His talent is not, on the evidence, for accumulating knowledge or for building organizations, but for occupying the center of a story. To write his biography is to write about a man who has spent seventy years arranging the world so that it will be written about him.

That is what makes this book both easy and hard to write. There is no shortage of material. There is, instead, an excess of noise, and the biographer's first task is to separate what can be documented from what merely circulates. The rest of this book is an attempt to do that.

Chapter 2
Queens

The Immigrant's Grandson

The Trump family fortune begins with a barber's son from a village in the Rhineland-Palatinate. Friedrich Trump was born in Kallstadt, in what is now Germany, in 1869. He emigrated to the United States at sixteen, found work as a barber in New York, and moved west, where he made money in the boomtowns of the Pacific Northwest and the Klondike gold rush, mostly by running restaurants and rooming houses, and, according to accounts of his time there, by catering to the appetites of prospectors. He returned to Germany, married, and tried to settle in Kallstadt. Bavarian authorities, who noted that he had left the country without performing military service, expelled him in 1905. He returned to New York with his wife and infant daughter, and died in the influenza epidemic of 1918, leaving an estate that his widow, Elizabeth, and his teenage son Fred would put to use.

Fred Trump, born in 1905, was a builder almost from boyhood. Barely out of high school, he was already constructing garages and small houses in Queens under his mother's name, since he was a minor. By the 1930s he was building single-family homes and, with the arrival of federal housing programs during the Depression and after, he found the source of much of his eventual wealth. The Federal Housing Administration guaranteed mortgages for builders who followed its standards, and Fred learned to work the agency with exceptional skill. He built vast, plain, well-managed apartment complexes in Brooklyn and Queens: Shore Haven, Beach Haven, and, in the early 1960s, Trump Village at Coney Island. He supervised costs with a miser's attention. He was known for reusing lumber and for haggling with suppliers over pennies.

His methods drew official scrutiny. In 1954, a Senate committee investigating abuses in FHA programs examined Fred's profits on the Beach Haven project and concluded that he had received government mortgage money in excess of his actual costs, a practice known as mortgage windfall. Fred testified in a manner that was combative but unremarkable; he was not charged. Woody Guthrie, who lived for a time in one of his developments, wrote verses criticizing him as a landlord. It was a first brush with the public reputation that would follow the family: rich, tough, and always at the edge of the rules.

Fred and his wife, Mary Anne MacLeod Trump, a Scottish immigrant who had arrived in New York in the 1930s, had five children. Maryanne, the eldest, later became a federal appeals judge. Fred Jr., known as Freddy, was born in 1938. Elizabeth followed. Donald arrived on June 14, 1946, and Robert, the youngest, in 1948.

The House in Jamaica Estates

The Trumps lived in a mock-Tudor house on Midland Parkway in Jamaica Estates, a prosperous enclave in Queens. The family was not old money and did not pretend to be. Fred drove himself to his office in Brooklyn and demanded that his sons spend summers doing work. Donald would later recall going out to construction sites and collecting empty soda bottles for the deposit, and, as a teenager, working alongside his father on job sites. His father insisted on discipline and results. The children were warned against laziness, extravagance and weakness.

The psychology of the household has been analyzed by many writers, most of them without direct evidence. What is documented is this. Fred Trump's expectations of his eldest son were exacting, and he pushed Freddy toward the family business in the belief that he would be its heir. Freddy, by all accounts, was a warm and easygoing man who did not have his father's ruthlessness, and who wished to be a pilot. He was made to feel that he was failing. He drank. He left the business, became an airline pilot for a time, and by the 1970s was struggling with alcoholism. He died in September 1981, at forty-two, of a heart attack linked to the disease. Donald, who was a young man in his thirties by then, has said many times that he saw what alcohol did to his brother and has never drunk or smoked. The lesson he seems to have drawn from Freddy's story, however, was not a gentle one. In his niece Mary Trump's 2020 memoir, a book that Trump and his family disputed and tried to block in court, the death of Freddy is presented as a formative wound, the point at which Donald learned that weakness was to be despised. That is the view of one family member with her own grievances. It should be read as such.

The other formative fact was money. From an early age Donald Trump knew that his father was wealthy, that he himself would be wealthy, and that the family's position depended on a set of relationships with builders, lenders, officials and politicians that his father maintained. The Trump organization was a family business in the truest sense. Its accounts, its property, its tenants and its lawyers were intertwined, and the children were gradually made owners of pieces of it by means of a series of legal arrangements designed, in part, to reduce taxes.

Kew-Forest and the Military Academy

Donald attended the Kew-Forest School in Forest Hills, a private institution with a reputation for order. He was, by the recollections of classmates and teachers gathered by biographers, energetic, pugnacious and often in trouble: a boy who would test authority and enjoy the result. The details, such as the story that he once dropped a cake or gave a music teacher a black eye, come from Trump himself and are unverified. What is clear is that by thirteen his parents judged that he needed a firmer hand. In 1959 he was sent to the New York Military Academy in Cornwall-on-Hudson, a boarding school where boys wore uniforms, drilled, and lived by rank.

The experience, according to Trump, was formative. He rose to the position of captain, played baseball, and by his own account learned to succeed within a competitive system. His teachers and classmates remembered a confident student, more interested in winning than in learning. He later described the school as the place that taught him about leadership.

It was also, in a way that would have consequences for the rest of his life, the setting for his first significant encounter with the draft. The Vietnam War was escalating during his high school years. He graduated from the academy in 1964 and enrolled at Fordham University in the Bronx, where he spent two years. In 1966, he transferred to the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, to which his family connections and a call from an admissions officer who knew his brother, by his own account, may have contributed. He graduated in 1968 with a bachelor's degree in economics.

The Draft

Trump received four student deferments between 1964 and 1968. In 1968, after graduating, he was classified as 1-Y, and later 4-F, unfit for service. The stated reason, in his own account given decades later, was bone spurs in his heels. His medical records from the period have not been publicly released in complete form, and he has offered varying accounts of the condition, including that it was temporary. In 2018, the New York Times reported that the diagnosis had been provided as a favor by a Queens podiatrist, Dr. Larry Braunstein, who was a tenant of Fred Trump's; the account rested on the recollections of Braunstein's daughters, who said their father had told them it was a favor. Trump has denied it. No contemporaneous document has emerged that settles the question.

It matters, less for the underlying facts than for the political reality it created. Trump was a draft-age man of privilege who did not serve during a war that killed some fifty-eight thousand Americans, and who, in the 2016 campaign, sparred with Senator John McCain, a war hero, and with the Gold Star family of Captain Humayun Khan. His critics saw an obvious hypocrisy in a man who avoided service but described the military with a proprietor's relish. His defenders replied that many Americans of his generation did the same, and that avoiding the draft was not a crime. Both statements are true, and both fail to resolve what the episode shows about Trump's view of obligation: that rules and burdens are fine for those who cannot avoid them.

Joining the Family Firm

Upon graduating, Trump joined the family firm, then known as Elizabeth Trump and Son, after his grandmother. He worked in his father's office in Brooklyn. He learned the operation of the vast rental portfolio, which by then comprised thousands of apartments across the outer boroughs. He also learned to work with the lawyers, and most importantly with the political fixers, who kept things running.

One of the first public tests of the enterprise came in 1973, when the United States Department of Justice sued the Trump Organization in federal court in Brooklyn, accusing it of discriminating against Black applicants for apartments in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The government's evidence included testers, one Black and one white, who had been treated differently when applying for the same apartment, and internal notations by rental agents that coded applications from Black prospective tenants with the letter C. Donald Trump, then twenty-seven, was president of the company in name and publicly defended it, saying that the government was trying to force the company to rent to welfare recipients. The Trumps retained a combative New York attorney named Roy Cohn, who counter-sued the government for defamation and demanded one hundred million dollars. The countersuit was thrown out. In 1975 the case ended in a consent decree in which the Trumps did not admit wrongdoing but agreed to take steps to ensure equal opportunity in renting, including advertising in minority-oriented publications and notifying the Urban League of vacancies. Later, the government charged that the company had violated the decree, and it remained a source of scrutiny.

Trump would say for the rest of his life that the case was settled without admission of guilt, which is technically true, and that the Justice Department had come after him unfairly. Critics pointed out that the government later alleged the company had fallen short of the decree's terms. The episode is important for two reasons. First, it established the pattern of legal combat that would mark Trump's career: attack the accuser, deny the charge, settle without admission. Second, it introduced him to Roy Cohn, whose influence would be profound and is the subject of a later chapter.

The Father's Money

How much did Donald Trump owe to his father? The question has been asked since the 1980s, and the answers have varied with the bias of the questioner.

Trump's account, given in many interviews and in his book The Art of the Deal, is that he started with a small loan of one million dollars from his father, which he paid back with interest, and that he built his business through his own talent. In 2015, at the announcement of his candidacy, he said it again: his father had given him a small loan, and he had turned it into billions.

In October 2018 the New York Times published the result of an investigation, based on tax records and other confidential documents, that presented a very different picture. According to the Times, Fred Trump had transferred to his children the equivalent of more than four hundred million dollars in today's terms over the course of his life, in part through arrangements that appeared to be designed to evade gift and inheritance taxes. The methods included undervaluing properties when transferring them, setting up a company called All County Building Supply and Maintenance that took a cut of purchases the family's buildings made, effectively passing money to the children, and other devices. In the mid-1970s, according to the Times, Donald Trump was receiving around two hundred thousand dollars a year from his father in his early adulthood; over the years the amounts grew. When Donald's casino ventures ran into cash trouble in 1990, Fred sent a lawyer to buy about three and a half million dollars in casino chips, which were not to be gambled; the transaction was a way to pass money to his son.

The White House at the time, and Trump himself, called the Times story a hit piece and said that the tax documents were inaccurate. New York authorities reviewed the story and the state tax department opened an inquiry, though no charges arose from it. The statute of limitations had run on most of the underlying conduct.

The truth appears to lie between the two extremes. Donald Trump was not a self-made man in the sense that he started with nothing. He started with a great deal: a father with money, guarantees, connections, and the willingness to bail him out. But he was also not merely a beneficiary. He took large risks that his father would not have taken, and he understood from very early that in Manhattan real estate, the deal that mattered was the one that changed how people saw you. Fred Trump built for tenants. Donald wanted to build for celebrity.

What the Boy Learned

If there is a lesson to draw from the Queens years, it is not psychological but practical. The young Donald Trump saw that government could be a partner and a patron for a builder who knew how to work it. He saw that lawyers could be weapons. He saw that a family could hold wealth as a fortress against taxes. And he saw, in the fate of his brother, what happened to those who did not fit his father's picture of a winner.

He also absorbed a way of talking about the world. To Fred Trump, the world was divided into killers and losers, and the only goal was to be the former. That vocabulary would become Donald's own, and its echoes are audible in his politics fifty years later. Some who have studied him think it explains the frequency with which he divides people into those who are with him and those who are against him, into winners and losers. Others think it is simply the vernacular of a certain kind of New York businessman, and that too much has been made of the childhood.

What is certain is that by the time he turned twenty-two, the young man from Jamaica Estates had all the tools he would need: a first-class education in the rules of a rough business, a father with deep pockets, an appetite for attention, and a gift for salesmanship. The one thing he did not yet have was Manhattan. In the next chapter we follow him across the East River.

Chapter 3
Across the East River

The Commodore

In the early 1970s New York City was a place that many people were trying to leave. The city was approaching bankruptcy, crime was rising, the subways were covered in graffiti, and entire neighborhoods burned. Mid-Manhattan real estate, which had been the safest asset class in the country, was in a slump. Office buildings stood half empty. Hotels were failing. It was, for a young man with confidence, a time of bargains, and Donald Trump, in his late twenties, understood that his father's outer-borough empire was not where the excitement was.

He began to spend time in Manhattan, taking an apartment on the Upper East Side, frequenting Le Club and other nightspots, and cultivating people who could introduce him to the city's power brokers. In 1973 he was introduced at Le Club to Roy Cohn, the lawyer whose notoriety as Senator Joseph McCarthy's chief counsel in the 1950s had never quite faded. That meeting, to be discussed in the next chapter, was among the most consequential of Trump's life. In 1974 Trump began to focus on a specific target: the Commodore Hotel, next to Grand Central Terminal on East 42nd Street.

The Commodore was an old, grimy, failing hotel owned by the bankrupt Penn Central Railroad. The neighborhood around Grand Central was seedy. The city was desperate for someone to invest in it. Trump saw in the building what he would later see in a hundred other places: a location that was better than the current use of it, and an owner that badly needed to sell.

The Deal

The Commodore transaction, completed in 1976 and opened as the Grand Hyatt in 1980, became the template for Trump's early career and is worth understanding in detail, because it shows how his method worked and who bore the risks.

Trump did not have the money to buy the hotel. What he had was an option on the property, which he obtained from Penn Central for about ten million dollars, and a claim to be the person who could bring a major hotel operator into the deal. He persuaded the Hyatt Corporation, run by the Pritzker family, to partner with him. Then he turned to the city. He needed a tax abatement, without which the hotel could not be profitable. The city owned no stake in the building, but the state's Urban Development Corporation could take title to it and lease it back to the developers, exempting it from property taxes for a period.

In the negotiations, Trump obtained a forty-year abatement, one of the most generous ever granted in New York. Under the arrangement, the developer would pay the city a fixed sum in lieu of taxes that rose with the hotel's profits. Mayor Abraham Beame, who was fighting a fiscal crisis, signed off. Fred Trump guaranteed a loan for the deal and helped to put Donald in front of key lenders, including the Equitable Life Assurance Society and Chase, and the elder Trump's reputation in the New York banking community was an important part of what made the whole thing possible. The New York Times, in a later account, said that Fred's guarantee was decisive in persuading the banks.

The hotel opened in 1980 as the Grand Hyatt New York. It was a success. It also made Trump a very wealthy man on paper, since he held a significant equity stake. The abatement, however, was for decades a source of criticism. Analyses of the deal by the city's Independent Budget Office and by journalists estimated that the tax break cost the city many millions of dollars over its life. Trump's defense was that the city had obtained a working hotel where none had existed and that the tax revenue from a failed hotel would have been zero.

What the Commodore showed was Trump's conviction that in New York, public money could be made to serve private developers, and that the trick was to structure the deal so that the risk sat with someone else. In this case, the risk sat with the city and with his father's guarantee.

Trump Tower

If the Commodore made Trump a player, Trump Tower made him a celebrity. The site was Bonwit Teller, an elegant Fifth Avenue department store. Trump acquired the air rights from Tiffany next door, assembled the plot, and negotiated another abatement, this one for a mixed-use tower with a public atrium. He partnered with the Equitable, which took half of the deal, and hired Der Scutt as architect. The building was to be a monument to luxury, and it was tall: fifty-eight floors by the height of the building's actual structure, though with taller ceilings on some floors and generous marketing, the tower was billed as sixty-eight stories.

Two episodes from the construction stand out. The first concerned the Bonwit Teller building's Art Deco limestone friezes, which the Metropolitan Museum of Art had expressed interest in acquiring. Trump initially said that he would donate them, but the friezes were destroyed during demolition. He said they were of no artistic value and would have cost too much to remove. Preservationists never forgave him.

The second episode concerned the demolition workers. In 1980, undocumented Polish laborers, known as the Polish Brigade, were paid low wages, worked long shifts, and in some cases slept on the site. The union benefit funds representing the demolition trades sued, and the litigation dragged on into the late 1990s. Trump testified that he did not know the workers were undocumented and has always maintained that he was unaware of it. Witnesses in the case said that Trump Organization managers on the site were aware of the workers and their pay, a claim Trump disputed.

Trump Tower opened in 1983. The building's success validated Trump's approach. The apartments, marketed to wealthy foreigners and celebrities, sold well. Retail tenants such as Gucci and Charles Jourdan paid premium rents. The atrium became a tourist attraction. And the building was covered in the publicity that Trump valued above all else.

The Concrete Club

There is another chapter in the story of Trump Tower, and it concerns the concrete. New York in the early 1980s was a city in which the concrete industry, like construction unions and much else, was substantially influenced by organized crime. A federal investigation in the mid-1980s, culminating in the prosecution of the heads of the Five Families, established that the Genovese and Gambino crime families had, through a cartel known as the Concrete Club, controlled the supply of ready-mix concrete for large construction projects in the city, exacting a tax on each yard poured.

Trump Tower was built of reinforced concrete, and the concrete was supplied by S&A Concrete, a company that was owned by Anthony Salerno, known as Fat Tony, boss of the Genovese family, and Paul Castellano, boss of the Gambinos, through fronts. Trump used S&A. The reporting on this by the New York Times and by later authors, including the journalist Wayne Barrett, whose 1992 book Trump: The Deals and the Downfall remains a landmark, shows that Trump also worked with the construction union leader John Cody, who was a criminal with ties to the mob, and that he obtained favorable labor peace on the site.

Trump has denied that he did anything improper, and he was never charged with any crime in connection with the concrete. The most defensible statement of what the record shows is that in the New York of the early 1980s, a builder of large concrete towers had almost no way to avoid dealing with companies that were mob-controlled, and that Trump, like other developers, did so. That is not evidence of a crime. It is evidence of the environment in which he learned his trade, and of his willingness to work with people he must have known were criminals.

The Rise of the Brand

By the middle of the 1980s, at the age of about forty, Trump had become one of the most famous businessmen in America. He was helped by his flair for getting attention. He was photographed with beautiful women, in penthouse rooms, on yachts. He gave interviews in which he boasted. He took out large advertisements. He acquired the New Jersey Generals of the United States Football League, and, in 1986, led the USFL's antitrust suit against the National Football League; the jury found that the NFL had violated antitrust law but awarded the league one dollar in damages, tripled under the statute to three dollars, a result that essentially ended the league.

At the same time he was building the persona that would define his public life. In 1987 he published The Art of the Deal, a business memoir written with the journalist Tony Schwartz. The book was a sensation, staying on the bestseller list for months, and it created Trump's public image as the ultimate dealmaker. Schwartz, who did most of the writing, later said he regretted his role, calling the book a work that had created a false picture of Trump as a successful business genius. In a 2016 interview with The New Yorker, Schwartz said that he believed Trump lacked the ability to focus, and that the book had presented him as more disciplined than he was. Trump has denied this.

The book taught that the way to succeed in business was to think big, to use leverage, to fight, and to promote yourself. It defined the notion of truthful hyperbole, a phrase Schwartz reportedly devised, to describe how Trump exaggerated: as an innocent form of sales puffery. Critics point out that the line between puffery and falsehood is exactly the one that Trump has been accused of crossing ever since.

The Bargain

The story of the rise of Donald Trump in Manhattan can be told as a triumph of talent and daring. The buildings are real. The Grand Hyatt is still standing; Trump Tower, which was his home and headquarters and later the site of his 2015 announcement, is still there, still in his family's hands. He did what most of his peers had not dared to do, and he did it in a time when the city was in trouble.

But it can also be told as a story about subsidy and leverage. The two great early projects were made possible by tax abatements and by his father's guarantees. The people who assumed the risk were not Trump. And the enterprise that emerged from them was built on an unstable foundation of debt and image, which would be put to the test in Atlantic City.

In the years after the Commodore, Trump's name became a brand. His appetite for that brand grew, and so did his indebtedness. The next chapter looks at the man who taught him the rules of the game he was playing, and whose mentorship would come to shape his character and his politics more than any other influence.

Chapter 4
Roy Cohn and the Rules of Combat

The Lawyer

In the autumn of 1973, a few months after the Justice Department filed its discrimination suit against the Trump Organization, Donald Trump was dining at Le Club, a members-only discotheque on East 55th Street, when a man at a nearby table was pointed out to him. He was a pale, heavy-lidded lawyer of forty-six with a reputation for ferocity, a bulging Rolodex, and a well-earned notoriety. Trump asked who he was, and was told: Roy Cohn. Trump reportedly said that he wanted to meet him. It was, as he later recalled, a chance meeting that turned into one of the most important relationships of his life.

Roy Marcus Cohn had been born in the Bronx in 1927 to a family with political connections. His father was a judge. He graduated from Columbia Law School at twenty, too young to be admitted to the bar, and had to wait for his birthday. He became a federal prosecutor and made his name in the prosecution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg for atomic espionage. He was later accused of improperly pressing the judge to impose the death sentence, a claim supported by documents that surfaced decades afterwards. In 1953 he became chief counsel to Senator Joseph McCarthy's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations and, with McCarthy, presided over the anti-Communist hearings that ruined many careers and were eventually censured. Cohn left Washington in 1954 and became a private attorney in New York, where he represented mobsters, Catholic archdiocese officials, real estate developers, and celebrities. He was indicted three times, in the 1960s and 1970s, on charges including bribery and fraud, and was acquitted each time.

Cohn's reputation was that he would do anything for a client. He was known to threaten opponents, leak damaging material to columnists, use every procedural delay, and never apologize. He was also, by all accounts, generous to those he liked: his loyalty was intense, and so was his vindictiveness. He was closeted and homophobic in public, and was in private engaged in a lifestyle that he never acknowledged. He would die of AIDS in 1986, still denying it, telling the world he had liver cancer.

The Tutor

Trump hired Cohn to defend the family in the discrimination suit. Cohn's advice, according to Trump's later reminiscences and to biographers, was to fight. The firm did not settle right away. Cohn filed a one-hundred-million-dollar countersuit alleging that the Justice Department had defamed the Trumps by accusing them of racism, a maneuver that was dismissed by the court. He also presented the defense in public, telling reporters that the government's case was a quota system in disguise. In 1975 the case was resolved by consent decree. The Trumps did not admit wrongdoing, and Cohn described the outcome as a victory.

More than the outcome, what Trump took from the experience was a style. Cohn's rules of combat, as they were described by people who knew him and by later writers, included the following. Always counterattack. Never admit fault. Never apologize. Claim victory no matter what happens. Use the press to shape the narrative, and use lawsuits as a weapon against enemies. Make your opponent the story.

Cohn was his attorney in the 1970s and 1980s for a variety of matters, including the drafting of a prenuptial agreement with Ivana Zelníčková, the Czech skier and model he married in 1977. Cohn's law firm also represented Trump's father, and Cohn and Trump spent considerable time together. Cohn's circle included the publisher Rupert Murdoch, the lobbyist Roger Stone, the political consultant Paul Manafort, and Cardinal John O'Connor of New York, and through Cohn Trump met Stone and Manafort. Stone and Manafort would later be at the center of Trump's political career, and both were, in the 1980s, partners in a lobbying firm, Black, Manafort, Stone and Kelly, that had Trump as a client.

There is a famous, possibly apocryphal, story in which Trump, discovering the extent of Cohn's illness in 1986, reportedly distanced himself from him. Accounts differ. Some say Trump stopped taking his calls; others that Trump remained loyal until the end. What is not disputed is that Cohn was disbarred by the New York courts in June 1986, shortly before his death, for unethical conduct including misappropriating client funds and lying on a bar application. Trump has said that Cohn was a great lawyer and, in his second term, has been reported to have asked, in moments of frustration, why he did not have a Roy Cohn of his own. The remark, attributed in a Times report of 2018 to Trump speaking to White House staff, has been widely quoted.

The Cohn Method in Practice

Cohn's approach can be seen in many episodes of Trump's later career, and the pattern is instructive. It should be stated fairly. Denying an accusation and attacking the accuser is not, in itself, dishonorable; it is what many defendants and their lawyers do. The question is whether it is applied to claims that are true.

Consider the way Trump has responded to serious allegations. When the Access Hollywood tape emerged in 2016, he issued an apology of sorts, and within hours, at the presidential debate, brought former President Clinton's accusers into the room. When women came forward with claims of sexual misconduct, Trump denied them all, called the accusers liars, and, in several cases, threatened to sue. When a jury found in 2023 that he had sexually abused and defamed the writer E. Jean Carroll, he said the verdict was a disgrace and repeated the statements about her that the jury had found defamatory, leading to a second jury award of more than eighty-three million dollars in 2024. When he was indicted, he called the prosecutors deranged and said the cases were election interference, and he made the prosecutors, judges, and their families targets of his political attacks.

The tactic has an element that goes beyond legal strategy. Cohn taught Trump that the public record is a battlefield and that the appearance of strength was strength. A man who said he was winning, regardless of the facts, was more effective than a man who told the truth and lost. The thing Trump absorbed was a lesson about power: that shamelessness is an asset, and that the person who never retreats is the person who eventually wins.

Cohn's Circle

Cohn's world was not confined to Trump. It included a cast of characters that had an outsized influence on the politics of the late twentieth century. Stone, who had worked on Richard Nixon's 1972 reelection campaign as a teenager and had a tattoo of Nixon on his back, brought to Trump an appreciation of political dirty tricks. Manafort, a Republican operative who had worked for Presidents Ford, Reagan and George H.W. Bush and later for foreign clients including the Ukrainian politician Viktor Yanukovych, was a fixer who knew how to combine lobbying with foreign money. In 1987 Stone was already urging Trump to run for president. Trump took the idea seriously enough to make a speech in New Hampshire that year, and stoked it for years, though it was not yet a real candidacy.

These names will recur. Manafort chaired Trump's 2016 campaign for a time and was later convicted of bank and tax fraud in a case brought by special counsel Robert Mueller; Stone was convicted of lying to Congress and obstructing an investigation, and both were pardoned by Trump. It is worth noting the depth of the relationship with these men and how long it dated back. The continuity between the Trump of 1980 and the Trump of 2016 is stark. He did not discover politics. He came to it with a group of advisers who were, in some cases, decades in his orbit, and who understood, as Cohn had, that the game was to intimidate and to control the story.

The Legacy

There are two ways of assessing Cohn's influence on Trump. The first is that it was decisive. In this view, Trump acquired from Cohn a philosophy of combat that he has applied in business, in politics and in the courtroom, and that explains a great deal of his conduct. He treats every dispute as a fight to be won, every critic as an enemy, every setback as an opportunity for a counterattack. He cannot lose, only be cheated. This view is put forward, among others, by the filmmaker Ivy Meeropol, granddaughter of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, in her documentary about Cohn, and by many journalists.

The second view is that the influence has been overstated. Trump was already, at twenty-seven, the son of a man who had spent his life in the ruthless world of New York property. He was already a fighter. What Cohn gave him was a lawyer's technique, not a personality. Trump has worked with dozens of attorneys, and has sometimes, particularly in the second term, complained that they have not been sufficiently aggressive. This view acknowledges Cohn's role while holding that Trump would have become Trump anyway.

The reader can decide. What is undisputed is that the rules attributed to Cohn have been observed with remarkable fidelity across fifty years. In every crisis of his career, from the casino collapses of the early 1990s to the criminal indictments of 2023, Trump has behaved as Cohn would have wished: he denied, he attacked, and he claimed to have won. Sometimes it worked. Sometimes it did not. But he has never stopped.

Chapter 5
Atlantic City

The Boardwalk Gamble

New Jersey legalized casino gambling in Atlantic City in 1976, hoping to rescue a decayed seaside resort. By 1980 the first casinos were open, and by the middle of the decade the city's Boardwalk was a corridor of glittering towers that took in hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Trump, already a Manhattan celebrity, saw a new frontier. He did not know the gambling business, but he knew what a casino required: a site, a license, a name, and financing. He set about assembling all four.

His first move was to acquire land on the Boardwalk. He then entered a partnership with Harrah's, the casino operator, and with the Holiday Inn chain, which had experience in the industry. The result was Harrah's at Trump Plaza, which opened in 1984. The partnership did not last. Trump bought out Harrah's stake within two years, and it became Trump Plaza. Meanwhile Trump acquired a half-finished casino hotel that Hilton had decided not to open after failing to obtain a license, and he opened it in 1985 as Trump Castle, a marina property. In 1988 he took over a project from Resorts International and completed it as the Trump Taj Mahal, which opened in April 1990 at a cost of well over one billion dollars, the most expensive casino built up to that time.

The Taj was the pivotal transaction. It was financed in large part with junk bonds, high-interest debt sold at a rate of fourteen percent. Even the casino's own analysts warned that the Taj would need to earn a level of revenue, about one million dollars a day, that no Atlantic City property had reliably achieved. Trump, ignoring the caution, said that the Taj would be the eighth wonder of the world. The New Jersey Casino Control Commission, which had to license Trump as a casino owner, found him financially qualified in 1989 only on the condition that his father's guarantees stay in place; and it noted with concern that he might be spreading his resources too thin.

The Empire on Credit

In the second half of the 1980s Trump embarked on the most aggressive buying spree of his career. He acquired the Eastern Air Shuttle, renamed the Trump Shuttle, with a loan of some three hundred and eighty million dollars, in 1989. He bought the Plaza Hotel in Manhattan in 1988 for about four hundred and seven million dollars, an amount that many observers considered too high. He acquired a yacht, the Trump Princess, from the Sultan of Brunei's brother, and he bought Mar-a-Lago, the sprawling Palm Beach estate built by Marjorie Merriweather Post, in 1985 for about ten million dollars. He began to build a portfolio of apartments and office towers.

Behind these purchases lay a simple financial reality. Almost all of it was bought with borrowed money, and much of the debt was personally guaranteed by Trump. In 1990, as revenue from the casinos failed to meet expectations, the Trump Organization struggled to make its payments. In a widely reported incident that summer, Trump was said to have been unable to pay interest of more than seventy million dollars on the bonds of the Taj, and a group of banks was brought in to negotiate. The details of what followed are recorded in the accounts of the banks and of the journalists, and they tell of a remarkable set of negotiations.

The banks faced a dilemma. Trump owed them roughly three billion dollars in loans, of which about eight hundred million he had personally guaranteed. If they foreclosed, they would take possession of properties that were worth less than they had lent, and they would face the reputational and practical difficulty of running casinos and a hotel. If they kept him going, they hoped that a recovery in the market would eventually let them recoup their money. In June 1990, a group of about seventy bankers agreed to a rescue plan. Trump was given a personal allowance to cover living expenses, reportedly of about four hundred and fifty thousand dollars a month. He was made to give up control of certain assets. Interest payments were deferred. His personal guarantees were reduced. The banks in effect kept him in business.

Trump has said throughout that the banks needed him, that he was smarter than they were, and that he had made the banks money. The bankers who worked on the deal said that his name was valuable and that liquidating him would have been harder. Both accounts contain something of the truth. Trump's line, that if you owe the bank a hundred thousand dollars you have a problem, but if you owe the bank a hundred million dollars the bank has a problem, was often quoted. In his case it turned out to be substantially true.

The Bankruptcies

Trump's casino companies filed for reorganization under Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code repeatedly. The Trump Taj Mahal filed in 1991. Trump's Castle and the Trump Plaza followed in 1992. In 2004 Trump Hotels and Casino Resorts filed, and in 2009 the successor company, Trump Entertainment Resorts, filed once more. In all, Trump-affiliated businesses have gone through six corporate bankruptcies, counting a separate 1992 filing for the Plaza Hotel.

Trump has said that this is a normal way of doing business and has claimed that he used the law as a tool, taking advantage of bankruptcy statutes to reduce debts and maintain control. This is true in a narrow sense. Chapter 11 reorganizations do not necessarily represent personal failure, and Trump did not personally file for bankruptcy; his personal finances were never formally adjudicated. Corporate law protects the personal wealth of owners from the debts of their companies except where they have guaranteed them. But investors and creditors paid a price. Bondholders in the Taj Mahal, who had lent money at high rates to a project sold on the strength of Trump's reputation, took losses, and so did the contractors and small businesses that were not paid in full. Lawsuits by subcontractors in Atlantic City alleged that Trump Organization companies had stiffed them; a 1990s suit by the contractor of the Taj Mahal, and a later series of claims, are documented in the reporting of the time. A USA Today investigation in 2016 found dozens of lawsuits and hundreds of liens filed against Trump's businesses by contractors and workers who said they had not been paid, though Trump's campaign disputed the accounting and said it was misleading given the scale of his operations.

Trump's defenders make a straightforward argument. The casino business was hard, they say, and many operators went bankrupt. The New Jersey market was oversaturated. Trump resigned from the board of the casino company in 2009, and he made money from fees and licensing. He did not lose his personal fortune, and he recovered to build one of the more prominent real estate businesses in the world. That is all true. What his critics argue is that his early reputation as a genius was not the result of profitable performance but of a marketing effort, and that the taxpayers, lenders and small businesses who had to deal with the results paid for it.

The Tax Returns

There is another piece of evidence about how Trump's early gains and losses translated into personal finance, and it comes from his tax returns. In October 2016, a few weeks before the election, the New York Times published pages from Trump's 1995 New Jersey state tax return, which had been mailed anonymously to a reporter. The documents showed that Trump had reported a loss of nearly nine hundred and sixteen million dollars in that year. Under the tax law of the time, such a loss could be used to offset income for up to eighteen years, and tax experts said that it could have allowed Trump to avoid paying federal income taxes for a long time.

Trump did not dispute the authenticity of the returns. He said that he had taken advantage of the tax code legally, as any smart businessman would. In the first presidential debate, when Hillary Clinton suggested that he had paid no federal income tax, he answered that it made him smart. The remark was seen as a rare admission and was widely replayed.

Trump broke with a forty-year tradition of presidential candidates by declining to release his tax returns, saying first that he was being audited, and later that voters did not care. In 2020, after a long legal fight, the New York Times obtained more than two decades of tax data and reported that Trump had paid just seven hundred and fifty dollars in federal income tax in 2016 and again in 2017, and no income tax at all in ten of the previous fifteen years. Trump called the story fake news and said he had paid millions of dollars in taxes, some of which was property tax and payroll tax. In November 2022, after the Supreme Court declined to block the release, the House Ways and Means Committee obtained six years of Trump's personal and business tax returns and made them public in December, confirming that Trump had paid little or no federal income tax in several years.

The Man and the Myth

There are two ways of reading the Atlantic City chapter of Trump's story. The first is as a tale of creative destruction. A young man took bold risks, sometimes failed, and always came back, which is what entrepreneurs do. The second is as a story about a certain kind of business practice: one in which reputation replaces profit, in which the losses fall on others, and in which the failure of one venture is never allowed to spoil the myth.

The evidence tends toward the second reading, at least for the casino years. In a business in which some operators made fortunes, Trump's casinos, taken together, were notably unprofitable. A 2016 analysis by the Washington Post and reporting by Bloomberg suggested that while Trump himself drew salaries and fees, the public companies that held his casinos lost large sums for shareholders. The Trump brand survived, and even thrived, because its value depended not on the results of any particular deal but on the perception that it stood for success.

The lesson of Atlantic City, for a man who would later run for office, was thus a curious one. It taught him that failure could be survived, that debts could be renegotiated, and that the public's memory was short. It also taught his critics that his claims about his own abilities should be tested against records. The banks that had kept him afloat in 1990 did not, on the whole, lend to him again for many years. In the 2000s he would turn to foreign sources, most notably Deutsche Bank, and to a different model of business, one that required less capital and carried less risk: putting his name on other people's buildings.

The next chapter turns from the collapse of the empire to the reinvention of its founder.

Chapter 6
The Reinvention

Tabloid Years

By 1990 Donald Trump was, in the eyes of the New York press, both a celebrity and a cautionary tale. The tabloids that had celebrated his rise now tracked his troubles with relish. The New York Post ran the most famous headline of his personal life in February 1990: Best Sex I've Ever Had, a quotation attributed to Marla Maples, describing an affair that was destroying his marriage to Ivana. The paper's treatment of the divorce, which played out over the following year, was a saga of details about the couple's finances, their prenuptial agreement, and the way Trump had, according to Ivana's court filings, treated her. In a sworn deposition in the divorce, Ivana alleged that Trump had assaulted her in 1989, an allegation that she later described as not intended literally, saying in a statement attached to the publication of a book about Trump that she did not want her words to be interpreted as a criminal accusation. Trump denied it. The couple settled in 1990, and Trump married Marla Maples in 1993, two months after the birth of their daughter Tiffany. That marriage ended in 1999.

Trump treated the coverage as an asset. He was, by his own account, willing to call reporters himself, and it has long been documented that from the 1980s he sometimes did so under an assumed name, John Barron or John Miller, praising Donald Trump and describing his romantic life. Trump acknowledged using the name John Barron in a 1990 deposition. In 2016 the Washington Post published a recording of a 1991 call to a People magazine reporter by a man calling himself John Miller; Trump denied that the voice was his, though the reporter and others said it was. It is a small example of a larger phenomenon. Trump has long treated the media as a machine for making him famous. What he seems to have understood from the beginning is that the press is less interested in the truth than in the story, and that a person who supplies a steady stream of exciting stories, true or not, will always have coverage. The lesson, which he applied ruthlessly, was that all publicity is good publicity, that the important thing is to be talked about, and that a bad story can be survived if it is replaced by a bigger one.

The Central Park Five

Not all of the tabloid years produced only embarrassment. One episode from 1989 remains among the most consequential and the least defended of Trump's public interventions. On the night of April 19, 1989, a twenty-eight-year-old white woman who worked as an investment banker was beaten, raped and left for dead while jogging in Central Park. The crime, which came to be known as the Central Park jogger case, was one of the most sensational of its era. New York in the late 1980s was gripped by fear of crime, and the attack seemed to symbolize the city's decay.

Police arrested a group of Black and Latino teenagers who had been in the park that night, some of whom had been involved in other assaults. After long interrogations, four of the boys, who were fourteen, fifteen and sixteen, gave videotaped statements implicating themselves and others. Five were tried and convicted: Antron McCray, Yusef Salaam, Raymond Santana, Kevin Richardson and Korey Wise.

On May 1, 1989, Trump paid roughly eighty-five thousand dollars for full-page advertisements in four New York newspapers. The headline read, in capital letters, Bring Back the Death Penalty. Bring Back Our Police. The text called for the city to hate the muggers and murderers, and said that they should be forced to suffer. It did not name the five, but it was clearly directed at them. The ads inflamed public opinion and, according to the lawyers who represented the accused, helped to poison the atmosphere in which they were tried.

In 2002, a convicted murderer and serial rapist named Matias Reyes, who was serving a life sentence, confessed that he alone had attacked the jogger. His DNA matched semen found at the scene. A review by the Manhattan District Attorney, Robert Morgenthau, concluded that the confessions of the five had been unreliable and inconsistent, and their convictions were vacated. In 2014 the city agreed to pay a settlement of forty-one million dollars to the five, who by then were men in their thirties, and who had served between six and thirteen years in prison.

Trump has never apologized. In 2014 he wrote an opinion piece in the New York Daily News calling the settlement a disgrace, and in 2016, during the presidential campaign, he said that the men had confessed and that some people believed they were guilty. In a 2019 interview he said that he still did not accept that they were innocent, and that there had been no apology from the city's police. The film director Ava DuVernay dramatized the case in a 2019 series, When They See Us. In 2025, several of the exonerated men were reported to have sued Trump for defamation over his remarks about the case during a 2024 presidential debate; Trump disputed the claims, and the litigation was unresolved at the time of writing.

The episode is important for several reasons. It reveals a consistent trait, the refusal to admit error even when confronted with overwhelming evidence. It shows his willingness to weigh in on the most inflammatory of subjects. And it shows how early in his public life he learned to appeal to fear.

Mar-a-Lago

In 1985, as noted earlier, Trump acquired Mar-a-Lago, the Palm Beach estate built in the 1920s by Marjorie Merriweather Post, for a price reported as about ten million dollars, including furnishings. The property, which was on the Atlantic shore and had a hundred and eighteen rooms, was a national historic landmark, and Post had intended to leave it to the federal government as a winter White House, but the government found it too expensive to maintain. Trump saw in it something else: a prime piece of land that could be developed, or, if not, a private playground.

His first plan was to subdivide the land and build houses. When neighbors resisted, he used a different tactic. In 1993, facing financial pressure, he turned the estate into a private club. The neighbors objected, and Trump, according to accounts by biographers and journalists, threatened to allow Black and Jewish people to become members of the club, which was then a pointed threat in a town with a history of exclusion. The town relented, and Mar-a-Lago opened as a club in 1995 with an initiation fee that was, at first, modest and later rose to hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The club became a moneymaker and, later, the political headquarters of a movement. It was also the location of the search of August 2022, in which federal agents seized boxes of documents marked classified, an episode that will be discussed in a later chapter.

Rebuilding

In the mid-1990s, Trump began to recover. He restructured his debts, sold assets including the Trump Shuttle, the yacht and the Plaza Hotel, and worked to shed his personal guarantees. With the help of a strong economy and a bull market in New York property, the buildings that he retained gained value. In 1996 he acquired a stake in the historic building at 40 Wall Street, in lower Manhattan, for a modest sum, and in 1997 he obtained control of it. It became a source of steady income. He won the rights to develop a large tract of land on the Hudson River known as Riverside South, which he later sold to Hong Kong investors. He acquired Trump World Tower, opposite the United Nations, and the tower's apartments sold at a profit.

He also began to explore another business: selling his name. In the 1990s and 2000s, Trump licensed his brand to developers and manufacturers. He put his name on hotels, condominiums, golf clubs, neckties, steaks, vodka, water, mattresses, and, from 2005 to 2010, a for-profit school called Trump University. Some of these ventures succeeded. Many did not. Trump Vodka, Trump Steaks, Trump Mortgage, and the Trump Shuttle are well-known failures. But the model, in which he assumed little of the financial risk and collected fees for the use of his name, was much less dangerous than the casino model. In the 2000s it produced steady income and made his name a global brand. Trump-branded buildings rose in Panama, Toronto, Istanbul, Manila, Dubai, and elsewhere. The Trump name signified, to many people abroad, the essence of American wealth.

The Question of Net Worth

There is one element of Trump's reinvention that would later become the subject of a major legal action, and it concerns how he described his wealth. Since the early 1980s Trump has claimed a level of wealth that other estimators have questioned. In 1982, when the first Forbes 400 list was published, Trump was listed with his father, at a combined net worth of two hundred million dollars, an estimate that Forbes's reporters later said was inflated, in part because Fred Trump's wealth was substantially less than Donald had implied. In 1984, Trump told Forbes that he had a net worth of nearly a billion dollars. The magazine's own estimate was much lower.

The pattern was consistent. Trump described his assets in glowing terms, and the journalists who tried to verify them found the numbers to be softer than claimed. The most famous example was the square footage of his Trump Tower penthouse. In 2017 Forbes reported that he had listed the apartment as thirty thousand square feet when it was actually about eleven thousand, an overstatement of almost three times. Overstatements of that kind were the core of what New York Attorney General Letitia James alleged, decades later, in a civil fraud suit that produced a judgment in 2024.

A word of caution here: the point is not that Trump was uniquely dishonest in promoting his properties. Real estate developers routinely use flattering measurements. The issue in the later litigation was whether the overstatements had been made to banks and insurers in the course of obtaining loans, which is a different and more serious matter. That question is taken up in Chapter Eighteen.

The Shape of the Comeback

By the end of the 1990s Trump was no longer in danger of bankruptcy. He was a much more disciplined businessman than he had been in the 1980s, in the sense that he had learned to avoid risk. He had also learned something about celebrity that would transform his life. He appeared on the radio show of Howard Stern, and as a guest in movies and on television, including a cameo in Home Alone 2, and he made a series of pronouncements on politics. In 1999 he formed an exploratory committee to seek the presidential nomination of the Reform Party, before dropping out in February 2000 after a fight over the party's direction and the presence of figures such as David Duke and Pat Buchanan, whom he called a Hitler lover and a bigot. He did not run.

At the turn of the century, he was a fixture of the New York scene, a billionaire by his own count, a merchant of glamour who had come through his troubles. All he needed was a bigger stage. Before he found it, the people around him had already begun to shape his story, and the next chapter turns to the family that has stood beside him, and sometimes against him, for half a century.

Chapter 7
Marriages and Children

A Family Business, Twice Over

The Trump family is at once a private household and a corporation, and for most of the last half century the two have been hard to tell apart. Its members have been employees, partners, spokespeople, advisers and, at times, government officials. To understand Donald Trump it helps to know the people around him, because they have shaped the decisions of his career, and because in both of his presidencies several of them have held roles in his administration or in the movement that supports it.

This chapter follows the family from his generation to the next. It is drawn largely from public records, from interviews and memoirs by family members and former associates, and from court filings. Some of these sources have their own interests, and the chapter notes where they do.

His Siblings

Donald Trump was the fourth of five children. His eldest sibling, Maryanne, born in 1937, became a prosecutor, then a federal district judge appointed by President Reagan, and in 1999 a judge of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where she served until she retired in 2019, shortly before an inquiry into her role in the family's tax arrangements could proceed. She died in November 2023, aged eighty-six. In 2020, secretly recorded conversations between Maryanne and her niece Mary Trump were made public, in which she criticized her brother in strong language, saying, among other things, that he had no principles. She did not dispute the authenticity of the recordings.

His sister Elizabeth, who worked in banking, lived a private life. His younger brother Robert, a business executive who had worked in the family firm, died in August 2020, at seventy-one, after a period of illness. Shortly before his death, Robert had gone to court to try to block the publication of Mary Trump's memoir, arguing that she had violated a confidentiality agreement she had signed in the settlement of a family dispute over the estate of Fred Trump. A judge freed the publisher to go ahead, and the book, Too Much and Never Enough, sold more than nine hundred thousand copies on its first day.

His eldest brother, Fred Jr., died in 1981, as described in Chapter Two. His daughter Mary, a clinical psychologist, was a source for the New York Times's 2018 reporting on the family's finances, a fact that was revealed in 2020, and which led to the family's estrangement. In her book, she offered a psychological portrait of her uncle that his family rejected. As she is a family member with her own grievances, her account must be read with caution, but her documents, which included tax records, were an important part of the evidence for the Times's investigation.

Ivana

In 1976, at the Montreal Olympics, Trump met a Czech skier and model named Ivana Zelníčková. They married in April 1977 in a ceremony at Marble Collegiate Church in New York. She had, by her account, considerable business talent. Ivana managed the design of the Trump Castle casino, and in the late 1980s took charge of the Plaza Hotel, at a salary of one dollar a year and, in Trump's words, all the dresses she could buy. She became a public figure in her own right, as a fixture of the tabloids and as an author and fashion entrepreneur.

The couple had three children. Donald Jr. was born in December 1977, Ivanka in October 1981 and Eric in January 1984. Ivana was, by many accounts, the parent who exercised discipline. She was also the one who taught the children Czech, and it was to their grandparents in Czechoslovakia that the children were sent for time in the summer.

The marriage ended after Trump's affair with Marla Maples became public in 1989 and 1990, a story broken by the New York tabloids. The divorce, settled in 1990 and finalized in 1992, was among the most heavily covered of its day. In sworn testimony, Ivana described a violent episode in 1989, which she later said she did not mean in a literal or criminal sense; Trump denied it. She received a settlement that included cash, the Connecticut estate and an apartment. She died in July 2022 at the age of seventy-three, at her home in Manhattan, after a fall on the stairs, according to the medical examiner. She was buried at Trump's golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey, a decision that reportedly had a tax advantage, since a plot on a property used as a cemetery may qualify for reduced property taxes.

Marla

Marla Maples, an actress from Georgia, met Trump in the late 1980s. They were married in December 1993 at the Plaza Hotel, two months after the birth of their daughter Tiffany. The marriage lasted less than six years. They divorced in 1999. Tiffany, who grew up largely in California with her mother, later graduated from Georgetown law school, and in November 2022 married Michael Boulos, a businessman whose father, Massad Boulos, was named in 2025 as a senior adviser to President Trump on African and Arab affairs.

Melania

In September 1998, at a party during New York's fashion week, Trump met a twenty-eight-year-old model from Slovenia, who worked in New York under the name Melania Knauss. She was born Melanija Knavs in 1970 in Novo Mesto and raised in Sevnica, in what was then Yugoslavia. They were married in January 2005, in Palm Beach, at a ceremony that included guests such as Bill and Hillary Clinton, Rudolph Giuliani, Katie Couric and Simon Cowell. Their son, Barron, was born in March 2006.

Melania has been the most private of Trump's wives. She kept largely out of the public eye during his first campaign, and in 2016 was embarrassed when portions of a speech that she gave at the Republican National Convention were shown to resemble passages in a speech by Michelle Obama in 2008; a staff writer took responsibility. As First Lady, she pursued an initiative called Be Best, focused on children, and was the subject of persistent speculation about her attitude toward the presidency. In June 2018, when she visited a shelter for migrant children in Texas, she wore a jacket with the words I really don't care, do u? on the back, and the statement was widely interpreted as directed at her critics, although her spokeswoman said that it had no hidden message.

Melania's public role in the second term has been smaller than in the first. She remained in New York during much of the early part of the term, and has spoken about issues such as online safety for children. Her memoir, Melania, appeared in 2024. In the campaign, she said that she supported a woman's right to choose, a position at odds with her husband's, and said that she did not want the government involved in the decision.

Donald Trump Jr., who was born in 1977, went to the University of Pennsylvania, worked in the family business, and spent the first term in the executive suite in New York, running the Trump Organization with his brother. He appeared on the Apprentice, and became a prominent voice for the family in politics, particularly on social media. He attended the Trump Tower meeting in June 2016. In the second term, he has campaigned on behalf of Republicans, become associated with the business of the family, and, with his brother, run ventures in fields such as private security, crypto and real estate. His partner, Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was named the ambassador to Greece in 2025.

She married the real estate developer Jared Kushner in October 2009, after converting to Judaism. They have three children. In the first term, both became senior advisers in the White House, a controversial arrangement that involved security clearances that were reportedly granted over the objections of career officials. Ivanka, who worked on policy relating to families and the workforce, also used a private email account for some government business, a matter examined by the House Oversight Committee. After the first term she moved with her family to Florida, and she did not take a formal role in the 2024 campaign or the second administration, saying that she wanted to focus on her family.

He married Lara Yunaska in 2014, and Lara Trump became, in 2024, co-chair of the Republican National Committee, and later took a job as a television host.
