He was a campaign figure in 2024, in the sense that his father credited him with having recommended that he appear on certain podcasts.

The Family in Government

In the first term, the family's role was extensive. Ivanka and Kushner were senior advisers. The president's sons ran his business. After the term ended, many members of the extended family, and their business associates, appeared in the second administration. Charles Kushner, Jared's father, who had been convicted of tax evasion, witness tampering and illegal campaign contributions in 2005, and whom Trump pardoned in 2020, was named ambassador to France. Massad Boulos, Tiffany's father-in-law, became a senior adviser. Lara Trump served at the RNC. Guilfoyle went to Athens.

The extent to which a president can place family and family associates in positions of influence, and the question of whether the family's business interests are separate from the affairs of the state, are of the kind that no law fully answers. Anti-nepotism statutes bar a president from appointing relatives to agencies under his control, but courts have held that this does not apply to the White House. The family, for its part, sees no conflict. The Trumps believe that loyalty is the most important quality in an associate, and that the family is the ultimate source of it.

Trump at Home

Those who have worked for Trump describe a household that operated by his rules. He sleeps little, according to his own account and those of his staff, watches a lot of television, and has for decades avoided alcohol and tobacco, a habit that he attributes to the example of his brother Fred. He eats fast food, is a devotee of Diet Coke, and enjoys golf, which he plays at his own courses. He has said that he does not exercise, believing that the body has a finite store of energy that exercise depletes. He is by most accounts a devoted grandfather, with ten grandchildren, and, according to some accounts, a father who was often absent from his children when they were young.

These details should not be overinterpreted. What the family record shows is that Trump's most important relationships have been ones of loyalty and rivalry, and that the boundaries between family, business and politics have never been drawn with any precision. It is a pattern that stretches back to his father, and there is no sign that it will change.

Chapter 8
You're Fired

Mark Burnett's Idea

In 2003 the British-born television producer Mark Burnett, who had created the hit series Survivor, was looking for a new show. His idea was a reality competition set in the business world, in which contestants would compete for a job with a major executive. Burnett needed a boss who could carry the show. He has said that he considered several candidates and that when he was introduced to Donald Trump, he realized that he had found someone who was, in effect, a brand that everyone knew.

The Apprentice premiered on NBC on January 8, 2004. Sixteen contestants competed in teams to complete business tasks, and each week the losing team met in a boardroom in which Trump would decide who to eliminate. He ended each elimination with two words that became a catchphrase: You're fired. The show was a hit, drawing more than twenty million viewers for its first season. Trump was paid, according to reports, tens of thousands of dollars per episode at first, rising over the years to as much as a million.

The value of the show was not the money. The Apprentice reinvented Trump for a generation that had not lived through the Atlantic City collapse. To viewers who had never heard of the Taj Mahal bankruptcies, he was a decisive billionaire who ran a corporate empire from a gilded tower. The show's opening sequence, a montage narrated by Trump, told a story of a man who had been broke, had come back, and now sat at the top of the world. The story was, as the previous chapters have shown, more complicated than that. But the show had no need to be accurate. It needed to entertain, and it did.

Several people who worked on The Apprentice have said that the show shaped Trump's image in the ways that mattered. Producers, in accounts published in later years, said that they were instructed to make Trump look decisive, and that his boardroom decisions were often shaped by the edit, not by any careful assessment of the contestants' business skills. Bill Pruitt, a former producer, wrote that the producers had turned an unglamorous businessman into a titan. Burnett has denied that the show gave a false impression of Trump. Whatever the case, the effect on Trump was enormous. The Apprentice ran for fourteen seasons, with celebrity editions, until 2015. It made Trump one of the most recognized people in America, and it gave him access to an audience of tens of millions who saw him each week in a role that had nothing to do with the truth of his business.

The Brand Machine

The success of the show led to a boom in Trump's licensing business. From 2004 onward he lent his name to a growing list of products and buildings. He got a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2007. His companies, run by his children Donald Jr., Ivanka and Eric, who were beginning to take on roles in the organization, pursued licensing deals around the world. The pitch to foreign developers was the same in each case. For a fee, and sometimes a share of the profits, Trump would let his name go on the building, and would provide marketing support, design guidelines and the occasional presence at the opening.

The resulting projects, from a Trump Ocean Club in Panama City to towers in Istanbul, Manila, Mumbai, Toronto and Baku, were often controversial. In some cases, the developers were people who later turned out to have questionable backgrounds. A Trump project in Azerbaijan, developed with a local partner whose family ties and alleged links to Iran's Revolutionary Guard were reported by the New York Times in 2017, raised questions among journalists about the source of its money; the Trump Organization said that it had no role in the development other than licensing, and the project was abandoned. A different case, in Toronto, was ultimately a financial failure in which buyers of condominiums sued. In the Trump SoHo in New York, the sales practices were questioned by the New York attorney general's office and the buyers were later given a settlement.

The critical facts about this phase of Trump's business are the following. First, he was no longer the risk-taker of the 1980s. He made money with little capital. Second, the business depended on reputation, and the Apprentice was the most effective advertising for it that he could have wished. Third, in many places, the people willing to pay for the Trump name were those who wished to be associated with wealth and power, and who sometimes had reasons to prefer opaque financial arrangements. Fourth, the business created a web of overseas financial interests that, once he entered politics, would become a source of conflicts of interest.

Trump University

Not every venture succeeded, and one of them ended in litigation that reached into the presidential campaign. In 2005 Trump and his partners founded the Trump Wealth Institute, later renamed the Trump University, to offer seminars on real estate investing. Despite the name, it was not accredited, and not a university; New York State education officials told the company in 2005 to stop using the word university, and it continued to do so anyway until 2010, when it stopped operating.

The pitch was simple. For a low fee, an attendee could go to a seminar, where the instructors, who Trump said were hand-picked by him, would offer the chance to buy more expensive programs. These cost thousands and sometimes tens of thousands of dollars. Former students said that they were pressured to put the costs on credit cards and that the instruction was of little value. Some said that they had been told that they would meet Trump, and that, in fact, they were photographed with a cardboard cutout.

In 2010 and 2013, respectively, a class of students in California and the New York attorney general, Eric Schneiderman, sued. Schneiderman alleged that the school had defrauded more than six thousand people of about forty million dollars. Trump countered, as was his custom, that the suits were baseless and political. In the California case, Judge Gonzalo Curiel of the Southern District of California presided. Trump, during the 2016 campaign, attacked Curiel repeatedly, saying that because the judge was of Mexican heritage he was biased on account of Trump's proposed border wall. Curiel had been born in Indiana. Speaker Paul Ryan called the remarks the textbook definition of a racist comment.

In November 2016, days after his election as president, Trump agreed to pay twenty-five million dollars to settle the cases, without admitting wrongdoing. Judge Curiel approved the settlement in 2018. The episode is instructive for what it reveals about how Trump treats the legal system: he attacked the judge, politicized the case, and settled once the political benefit of resisting had ended.

Birtherism

If Trump University was an embarrassment, the birther campaign was something darker. In 2011, as the presumptive Republican field for the 2012 election began to form, Trump seized on a conspiracy theory that had circulated on the fringes since 2008: that President Barack Obama had not been born in the United States and was therefore ineligible to be president. The claim had been repeatedly debunked. Hawaii officials had confirmed Obama's birth certificate, and two Honolulu newspapers had published announcements of his birth in 1961.

Trump, however, made himself the leading voice of the movement. In appearances on television, including on The View and on Fox News, he said that he was skeptical, that he had people in Hawaii investigating, and that they were not finding what they expected. He said that he wanted to see the long-form birth certificate. In April 2011 Obama released the long form, and shortly afterward, at the White House Correspondents' Dinner, mocked Trump before an audience that included the man himself. Trump has been said by associates to have been furious, and some have suggested that the humiliation increased his determination to run for president. Whether that is true, the more relevant point is that Trump never stopped for the next five years to raise doubts about Obama's birth. Only in September 2016, under pressure from his campaign, did he state that President Obama was born in the United States, adding in the same breath that Hillary Clinton had started the rumor, which was not true.

The birther campaign has been seen by many historians as a formative event in Trump's political career. It showed that there was an audience for conspiracy theories and for a politician who would legitimate them. It also relied, in the judgment of many observers, on a racial subtext: the suggestion that the first Black president was somehow not truly American. Trump has rejected the accusation, and supporters have said that he was simply asking questions. But the campaign remains the clearest example of a pattern that was to become the trademark of his politics, in which a claim that is false is repeated until it becomes an accepted point of dispute.

The Political Apprenticeship

Through these years, Trump took a growing interest in politics. He made donations to politicians of both parties, including Hillary Clinton, who attended his 2005 wedding to Melania Knauss, the Slovenian-born model. He publicly debated running for office several times. He registered as a Republican, a Democrat, an independent and a member of the Reform Party at various times. He gave speeches to conservative gatherings, and in his public statements he warned repeatedly about the perils of trade with China.

In 2012 he endorsed Mitt Romney in a ceremony at his hotel in Las Vegas. After Romney's defeat, Trump tweeted that the election was a total sham and a travesty of a democracy, and encouraged his followers to march on Washington and stop this travesty. The tweet was later deleted. It is one of the earliest instances of a pattern that would recur.

In 2013 he spoke at the Conservative Political Action Conference and made visits to Iowa, an early primary state. In 2014 he reportedly told his staff to prepare for the possibility of a run. In 2015, just before his announcement, his aides believed that the decision was still uncertain. That was about to change, at the foot of a golden escalator in Trump Tower.

Chapter 9
The Escalator

June 16, 2015

At eleven in the morning on June 16, 2015, Donald and Melania Trump rode the gold-plated escalator down into the atrium of Trump Tower, past the waterfall and the marble, and into a crowd of supporters, some of whom, according to reporting the campaign disputed, had been paid a small fee to attend. Trump took the stage and announced that he was running for president of the United States. The speech, which lasted forty-five minutes and was largely unscripted, began with a comment on the state of the country and ended with a promise to make America great again.

It was in the middle of the speech that Trump said the words that dominated the coverage. Speaking of immigration from Mexico, he said that the Mexican government was sending people who had lots of problems, that they were bringing drugs, that they were bringing crime, and that some, he assumed, were good people. He said that they were rapists. The remarks were denounced by Republicans and Democrats, by business partners including Univision and NBC, which cut ties with him, and by a chorus of commentators who predicted that his candidacy was already over.

They were wrong. The remark, which Trump refused to retract, became the foundation of his campaign. To his critics it revealed racism. To his supporters it was proof that he would say what others were afraid to say. Whatever it revealed, it established what was to be the central dynamic of the next year: Trump would say something outrageous, the establishment would denounce him, his supporters would rally, and his poll numbers would go up.

The Field

In the summer of 2015, the Republican field was crowded, with seventeen major candidates competing for the nomination. It included governors and senators with experience, among them Jeb Bush, the former governor of Florida and the brother and son of presidents, who was expected to be the front-runner and had raised more money than any rival; Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz, senators from Florida and Texas; Scott Walker of Wisconsin; John Kasich of Ohio; and Chris Christie of New Jersey. Each of them had a theory about how to win. None of them anticipated what Trump would do.

He did not seek the endorsement of the party's donors, or appear to prepare, or follow the rules. At the first debate, on August 6 in Cleveland, the Fox News moderator Megyn Kelly asked him about his history of insulting women, whom he had called fat pigs, dogs, slobs and disgusting animals. Trump said that the only person he had called a name was Rosie O'Donnell, and added, to laughter, that he had been nice to her. The following day, he told CNN that Kelly had blood coming out of her eyes, or wherever, an insult that was widely interpreted as a reference to menstruation. He denied it. The feud with Fox News went on for months.

He mocked the appearance of the businesswoman Carly Fiorina, called Senator Cruz a liar and Senator Rubio little Marco, and gave Jeb Bush the label low energy. He told supporters at a rally that Senator John McCain was not a war hero, because he liked people who weren't captured. He questioned whether Cruz, who was born in Canada, was eligible for the presidency. Time after time, commentators said that he had gone too far. Time after time, his numbers held.

He also had a genius, which his rivals lacked, for the free media. By one estimate from the media analytics firm mediaQuant, Trump's campaign received nearly two billion dollars in free coverage during the primary campaign, about as much as all of the other candidates combined. Television networks discovered that broadcasting his rallies produced high ratings, and Leslie Moonves, then chairman of CBS, said in February 2016 that the campaign might not be good for America, but it was damn good for CBS.

Message and Movement

Behind the theater was a message that was more coherent than it seemed. Trump proposed to build a wall on the Mexican border, and to make Mexico pay for it. He promised to deport millions of undocumented immigrants. In December 2015, after the San Bernardino shooting by a couple who claimed allegiance to ISIS, he called for a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States, a proposal that was denounced widely and later modified. He criticized free trade agreements, especially the North American Free Trade Agreement, and promised to bring back manufacturing jobs, a message that appealed strongly to workers in the Rust Belt. He said that he would not cut Social Security or Medicare, in contrast to his rivals. He said that the American military had been depleted and that the country's allies were freeloading. He said that the political system was rigged.

The message was unusual for a Republican in several respects. It broke with the party's orthodoxy on trade, on entitlements, and on foreign wars, and it was expressed in a style of open aggression that a Republican candidate had rarely used. Analysts have debated whether the movement that followed was driven primarily by economic anxiety, cultural grievance, racial resentment, or partisanship. The best evidence suggests that all of these played a part. Studies of the 2016 electorate found that attitudes on race and immigration were strongly associated with support for Trump in the primaries, but also that many of his voters were people who had suffered from the decline of manufacturing, and that some had voted for Obama.

Winning the Nomination

Trump won the New Hampshire primary in February 2016 with thirty-five percent of the vote, after losing Iowa to Cruz. He won South Carolina and Nevada. On Super Tuesday, March 1, he won seven states. A last-minute effort by the establishment to stop him, with Rubio and Romney attacking him, failed. In March Trump got into a public dispute with Cruz over the appearance of their wives, and in May, after winning Indiana, he became the presumptive nominee. Cruz and Kasich withdrew. The Republican National Convention in Cleveland in July nominated him and Governor Mike Pence of Indiana, who was chosen to reassure evangelical voters and party regulars, as his running mate.

At the convention, Trump said that he alone could fix the country's problems, and his speech, drafted with the assistance of his advisers, described a nation in crisis. Ivanka Trump made the case for her father's character. Cruz refused to endorse him and was booed. Trump had won the nomination in less than fourteen months without ever having held elected office.

Clinton

His opponent was Hillary Clinton, the former First Lady, senator from New York and secretary of state, who had defeated Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont for the Democratic nomination after a long and sometimes bitter primary. Clinton was better prepared for the job, more experienced, and better funded. She was also a historically unpopular candidate, weighed down by the scandal over her use of a private email server while she was secretary of state, which the FBI director James Comey described in July 2016 as extremely careless but not criminal.

The contest between the two, in a country divided along lines of geography, education and race, was extraordinarily bitter. Trump called her Crooked Hillary. At rallies, supporters chanted Lock her up. He suggested, in August, that gun-rights supporters might do something about Clinton's judicial appointments, a comment that the Secret Service reportedly took seriously. Clinton said that half of Trump's supporters could be put into what she called a basket of deplorables, racist, sexist, homophobic, xenophobic, Islamophobic, and later apologized for putting it in that way. Her campaign focused on Trump's temperament, and ran ads with children watching Trump's words on television.

Trump won the debates, in the view of some, on style, and lost them, in the view of the polls, on substance. In the first debate in September, he interrupted Clinton constantly, and afterwards polls said that she had won. In the third debate, asked whether he would accept the results of the election, he said that he would keep the country in suspense. It was an early sign of a theme that would return, in a more dangerous form, four years later.

The Trump Campaign and Its Finances

The economics of the Trump campaign were unusual. He lent his campaign about fifty million dollars in the primary and then, for the general election, turned to donors, raising money through small contributions and through joint fundraising committees with the Republican National Committee. His campaign spent much of its money at businesses he owned, including his hotels, his airline and his properties. According to analyses by the Federal Election Commission filings and by news organizations, the campaign paid millions of dollars to Trump's own companies over the course of the race. The campaign said that these were normal rates for services provided.

His organization was small and often chaotic. He had three campaign managers in a year. Corey Lewandowski, who ran it initially, was fired in June 2016 after a controversy over his treatment of a reporter and his dispute with other advisers. Paul Manafort, the veteran operative who had been Roy Cohn's associate, took over, and was forced out in August after reports about his work in Ukraine. Steve Bannon, the head of the news site Breitbart, and Kellyanne Conway, a pollster, took over. Bannon, who described the campaign as a movement, brought a philosophy of economic nationalism and confrontation with the establishment.

The Result

On November 8, 2016, Trump won. He carried Florida, Ohio, Iowa, North Carolina, and, unexpectedly, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, states that had voted for Democrats in every presidential election since the 1980s. His combined margin in those three states was about seventy-eight thousand votes. He received three hundred and four electoral votes to Clinton's two hundred and twenty-seven, after seven electors defected from their pledges; the pledged tally had been three hundred and six to two hundred and thirty-two. Clinton won the popular vote by almost three million votes, or about two point one percentage points.

The election was a shock to nearly all professional observers. Nearly every poll had predicted a Clinton victory. Some of the explanations that were later offered for the outcome include the effect of the FBI Director James Comey's letter to Congress on October 28, 2016, in which he announced that the bureau was reviewing additional emails related to the Clinton investigation; the low turnout among Black voters and in some Democratic cities; the strength of Trump's showing among white voters without a college degree; and the failure of Clinton's campaign to spend enough time in the Midwest. It was also the case that Trump was helped by Russian interference, though how much is unknowable.

Trump himself could scarcely believe it, according to those who were with him on election night, and neither could his wife. The president-elect who took the stage at about three in the morning at the New York Hilton was a subdued and gracious man. It would not last, for the same election was the start of a series of investigations that would preoccupy his presidency, and those are the subject of the next chapter.

Chapter 10
The Tape, the Dossier, and the Investigation

October 7, 2016

On the afternoon of Friday, October 7, 2016, the Washington Post published a video and transcript of a conversation recorded in 2005, during a bus ride to the set of a soap opera on which Trump was to make a cameo. The tape, from the entertainment program Access Hollywood, captured Trump speaking with the host Billy Bush in vulgar terms about women. In the recording, Trump described attempting to seduce a married woman, and said that when you are a star, they let you do it, and that you can do anything, including grabbing women by the genitals.

The tape emerged less than five weeks before the election, and many in the Republican Party thought it would end his campaign. Trump released a video statement at about midnight, in which he said that the words were a distraction from the important issues, that he had said and done things he regretted, and apologized if anyone was offended. He also said that Bill Clinton had abused women, and that Hillary Clinton had bullied his victims. At the debate two days later he brought some of Bill Clinton's accusers to the room. Several dozen Republican officials withdrew their endorsements, and some called for him to step down as the nominee. He did not.

In the following days, at least ten women came forward with accusations of sexual misconduct against Trump, including allegations of groping and kissing without consent. Trump denied all of them, described the accounts as fabrications, and suggested that the accusers were not attractive enough for him to assault. He said he would sue the women after the election, and did not.

The Access Hollywood tape remains a marker in the history of the 2016 campaign, for reasons that go beyond the content. It showed a candidate who was not damaged by information that would have destroyed almost any other politician in the American past. The effect on the voters who supported him was, on the evidence of polls, small. The tape was, in the end, priced in.

The Silence Money

While the tape circulated, a second matter was unfolding, which would later produce criminal charges. The adult film performer Stephanie Clifford, who worked under the name Stormy Daniels, said that she had had a sexual encounter with Trump in 2006, after meeting him at a celebrity golf tournament in Lake Tahoe. Trump denied it. In the closing weeks of the campaign, Trump's personal attorney and fixer Michael Cohen arranged for Daniels to be paid one hundred and thirty thousand dollars in exchange for her silence. Cohen later said that he paid the money on Trump's instructions, and that the payment was designed to prevent the story from damaging the campaign.

A similar arrangement had been made with the former Playboy model Karen McDougal. The publisher of the National Enquirer, American Media Inc., whose chief executive David Pecker was a friend of Trump's, paid McDougal one hundred and fifty thousand dollars for the rights to her story and then did not publish it, a practice known as catch and kill. The Enquirer also paid a doorman at Trump Tower, who had a story about a child that Trump had allegedly fathered, and killed that story too; the publisher's own review found the claim not credible. Prosecutors later described the Pecker arrangement as a conspiracy to promote Trump's candidacy by suppressing negative stories.

In 2018, Cohen pleaded guilty in federal court to eight felonies, including campaign finance violations relating to the payments to Daniels and McDougal. He said that he had acted at the direction of Trump, identified in court papers as Individual-1. Trump denied that he had directed the payments. The Justice Department did not charge him, in keeping with its policy against indicting a sitting president. The state of New York did, in 2023, and the consequences are described in Chapter Eighteen.

The Russian Question

While the campaign was under way, another story was building. In June 2016, the Democratic National Committee announced that its computer network had been hacked, and cybersecurity researchers attributed the intrusion to Russian intelligence. In July, on the eve of the Democratic National Convention, WikiLeaks published thousands of internal DNC emails, which revealed that party officials had favored Clinton over Sanders. In October, WikiLeaks began publishing the emails of Clinton's campaign chairman John Podesta.

At a press conference in Florida on July 27, Trump said that he hoped Russia would find the thirty thousand emails that had been deleted from Clinton's private server. Russia, if you're listening, he said, I hope you're able to find the thirty thousand emails that are missing. I think you will probably be rewarded mightily by our press. He later said that he had been joking.

In January 2017, the intelligence community, in an assessment by the CIA, FBI and NSA, concluded with high confidence that Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered an influence campaign aimed at the U.S. presidential election, to undermine public faith in the democratic process, denigrate Clinton, and harm her electability, and that Putin and the Russian government had developed a clear preference for Trump. Trump said the assessment was a witch hunt and refused for some time to accept it. The bipartisan Senate Intelligence Committee, under a Republican chairman, later endorsed the conclusions of the assessment, in a report published in five volumes between 2019 and 2020.

The other element that became the subject of prolonged controversy was a series of reports that were compiled by a former British intelligence officer, Christopher Steele, for the opposition research firm Fusion GPS, which was paid by a law firm working for the Clinton campaign and the DNC. The Steele dossier, as it came to be called, alleged extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russia, and lurid claims about Trump's personal conduct in Moscow. BuzzFeed published the dossier in January 2017. Much of it has not been corroborated, and some of it was later discredited. The Justice Department's inspector general, Michael Horowitz, found in 2019 that the FBI had made serious errors in the applications to surveil the former Trump campaign adviser Carter Page, including relying on Steele's information without adequate checks, and had omitted exculpatory facts. Later, a special counsel appointed by Trump's Justice Department, John Durham, produced a report in 2023 that criticized the FBI for opening the investigation into the Trump campaign on the basis of thin evidence, though his prosecutions of individuals largely failed in court.

Comey and the Special Counsel

Trump took office on January 20, 2017. Within days, the FBI was pursuing an investigation into whether members of his campaign had coordinated with Russia. His national security adviser, retired General Michael Flynn, resigned after less than a month, because he had lied to Vice President Pence about conversations with the Russian ambassador. He later pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI.

On February 14, according to notes made by FBI Director Comey at the time, Trump asked him in the Oval Office to drop the investigation into Flynn, saying that he hoped that Comey could let it go. Comey did not. On May 9, Trump fired him. In an interview with NBC's Lester Holt, Trump said that he had been thinking about the Russia thing with Trump and Russia when he decided to do it. He also told Russian officials in the Oval Office that the firing had relieved great pressure on him.

The firing led directly to the appointment of a special counsel. On May 17, 2017, Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein appointed Robert S. Mueller III, the former FBI director, to investigate Russian interference and any links or coordination between the Russian government and individuals associated with the Trump campaign. Attorney General Jeff Sessions had recused himself from the matter, a decision that made Trump furious. Trump called the investigation a witch hunt repeatedly, in speeches and on Twitter.

Over the next two years, Mueller's office charged thirty-four people and three companies. The cases included Manafort, who was convicted in 2018 of eight counts of tax and bank fraud in a federal court in Virginia and then pleaded guilty to conspiracy in a second case; Rick Gates, his deputy, who pleaded guilty and cooperated; Flynn; George Papadopoulos, a campaign adviser, who pleaded guilty to lying about his contacts with a professor who said that the Russians had dirt on Clinton; Roger Stone, who was convicted in November 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstruction; and twenty-six Russian nationals and three Russian companies charged with hacking and social media manipulation. Cohen pleaded guilty in a separate prosecution by the U.S. Attorney's office in Manhattan.

The Mueller Report

Mueller delivered his report to the Attorney General, William Barr, in March 2019. Barr released a four-page summary that said that the investigation had not established that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government, and that Mueller had not reached a conclusion on obstruction of justice, leaving it to Barr, who concluded that the evidence was not sufficient to establish it. Trump declared complete and total exoneration.

The redacted report, published in April, told a more complicated story. Its first volume detailed the Russian operation and described many contacts between people close to Trump and Russians, including a meeting at Trump Tower on June 9, 2016 between Donald Trump Jr., Jared Kushner, Manafort and a Russian lawyer who had promised damaging information on Clinton. When told of the offer in an email, Trump Jr. had replied that if it's what you say I love it. The report concluded that the evidence was not sufficient to charge a criminal conspiracy, in part because some people had lied or deleted evidence, and it said that the campaign had expected to benefit electorally from information stolen and released through Russian efforts.

The second volume set out ten episodes in which Trump might have obstructed justice. These included his firing of Comey, his request to Flynn's case, his directive to the White House counsel Donald McGahn to have Mueller removed, which McGahn had refused to carry out, and his attempts to influence Sessions to limit the investigation. The report said that because of a Justice Department policy against indicting a sitting president, Mueller had not considered whether to charge him; it added that if the office had confidence that the President clearly did not commit obstruction of justice, it would have said so, and that it was unable to reach that judgment. In his public statement in May 2019, Mueller said that the report did not exonerate the president.

The report's conclusions were disputed then and are disputed still. Trump's defenders say that the investigation found no conspiracy, that the Steele dossier was a partisan fabrication that the FBI wrongly relied on, and that the special counsel had spent two years and tens of millions of dollars in pursuit of a story that turned out to be false. His critics say that the report documented extensive misconduct, that the president's own conduct in response to the investigation was the subject of the second volume, and that Barr's summary misled the public about its findings. A federal judge, Reggie Walton, said in 2021, in a public records case, that Barr had distorted the findings. The truth is that both claims can be true at once.

What the Investigation Meant

In retrospect, the Russia investigation shaped Trump's understanding of the government he now led. He came to believe that the FBI and the intelligence agencies had been used against him, that his enemies inside the government were engaged in a plot, and that the press was complicit. This view, which later became the animating idea of his second term, was supported by real findings, such as the Horowitz report and the Durham report, but was also greatly exaggerated in Trump's telling. In his mind the Mueller investigation and the later prosecutions were part of the same continuous effort to drive him from public life.

Nearly every major controversy of the first term, from the firing of Comey to the pressure on Ukraine, can be traced back to this belief. It is the thread that connects the events described in the chapters ahead.

Chapter 11
The First Term

The Inauguration and the Crowd

Donald Trump was sworn in on January 20, 2017, on the West Front of the Capitol, in a speech that his own supporters, and some of his critics, considered darker than the usual inaugural address. He spoke of carnage in the nation's cities, of rusted-out factories scattered like tombstones, and of an establishment that had protected itself but not the citizens of the country. From this day forward, he said, it's going to be only America first.

The next day, at the direction of the president, his press secretary Sean Spicer told reporters that the crowd at the inauguration had been the largest audience ever to witness an inauguration, period, both in person and around the globe. Photographs and Metro ridership data showed that it was smaller than the crowd in 2009 for Barack Obama. Asked on television the next day about the discrepancy, Trump's counselor Kellyanne Conway defended Spicer by saying that he had given alternative facts. The phrase became an emblem of the new administration's relationship with verifiable reality.

The Washington Post's fact-checking team, which had begun counting Trump's false or misleading statements at the start of his presidency, recorded thirty thousand five hundred and seventy-three of them over four years, an average of about twenty-one a day, with the rate rising toward the end of his term. Trump has said that the count was biased. But whatever one thinks of the methodology, the count reflects an established fact: Trump made more statements that were untrue than any American president in the modern era, and made them with a frequency that scholars of political communication found unprecedented.

The Agenda

In the first year Trump signed an unusual number of executive orders and moved quickly in some areas. Within a week of taking office he issued an order banning entry of citizens of seven Muslim-majority countries, which caused chaos at airports and was blocked by federal courts. A revised order was also blocked. A third version, which added North Korea and some Venezuelan officials and dropped some countries, was upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2018, in Trump v. Hawaii, by a vote of five to four.

He withdrew the United States from the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement, and from the Paris climate accord, announced in June 2017. He moved the U.S. embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. He withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran, and imposed sanctions. He began a trade war with China, imposing tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars in Chinese imports; he also imposed tariffs on steel and aluminum from allies. In late 2018 he reached a new trade deal with Mexico and Canada, the USMCA, which replaced NAFTA and took effect in 2020. He held summits with North Korea's Kim Jong Un, in Singapore in 2018 and Hanoi in 2019, and became the first sitting president to step across the border into North Korea. No lasting agreement on nuclear weapons emerged.

In the summer of 2018 his administration adopted a zero-tolerance policy at the southern border, under which adults crossing illegally were prosecuted, and as a result thousands of children were separated from their parents. The policy was widely condemned, including by many Republicans, and Trump ended it by executive order in June, after public outcry. A later inspector general's report and court proceedings established that the government had not kept adequate records of the separated families, and years afterwards hundreds of children had still not been reunited with their parents.

Taxes, Regulation and the Courts

The signature legislative achievement of the first two years was the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, signed in December 2017, which cut the corporate tax rate from thirty-five to twenty-one percent, reduced individual rates, doubled the standard deduction and, in some circumstances, allowed a deduction for pass-through business income. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that it would add about one and a half trillion dollars to deficits over ten years. Supporters credited it with encouraging investment and job growth; critics said that the benefits went disproportionately to corporations and the wealthy, and that the promised surge in wages was modest. Trump's efforts to repeal the Affordable Care Act failed in July 2017, when Senator John McCain cast the decisive vote against repeal, with a dramatic thumbs-down gesture.

His administration rolled back regulations across the government. It eased environmental rules, including limits on power plant emissions and vehicle fuel standards, weakened rules governing financial firms, and sought to cut immigration in nearly every category. It also pushed to expand fossil fuel production.

The most lasting legacy of the first term was almost certainly in the judiciary. Working with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who had refused in 2016 to consider President Obama's nominee Merrick Garland, Trump appointed three justices to the Supreme Court: Neil Gorsuch in 2017, Brett Kavanaugh in 2018, after a bitter confirmation fight in which Christine Blasey Ford accused him of sexual assault when both were in high school, an accusation he denied, and Amy Coney Barrett in October 2020, days before the election, after the death of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. He also appointed more than two hundred federal judges, including fifty-four to the courts of appeals, and shifted the courts to the right. In 2022 the Supreme Court, with the three Trump appointees in the majority, overturned Roe v. Wade in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, ending the constitutional right to abortion that had stood for nearly fifty years.

Charlottesville

The event that most damaged Trump's standing in the first term was not a policy but a remark. On August 12, 2017, white nationalists and neo-Nazis gathered in Charlottesville, Virginia, for a rally, ostensibly to protest the planned removal of a statue of Robert E. Lee. They marched with torches on the University of Virginia campus the night before, chanting slogans including Jews will not replace us. During the rally, a man who had participated, James Alex Fields Jr., drove his car into a crowd of counter-protesters, killing Heather Heyer, thirty-two, and injuring dozens of others.

Trump's first statement condemned hatred, bigotry and violence on many sides, on many sides. Two days later, under pressure, he read a statement that named the Ku Klux Klan and neo-Nazis. But on August 15 in the lobby of Trump Tower, in an impromptu press conference, he returned to his initial position. He said that there had been very fine people on both sides. He also said that the neo-Nazis and white nationalists should be condemned totally. The exact interpretation of the remarks has been contested ever since. Trump's defenders point to the sentence in which he condemned neo-Nazis and white nationalists, and say that his reference to fine people was about those who wanted to protest the removal of the statue. His critics answer that the marchers on the night before had been neo-Nazis, and that he did not distinguish between the groups. What is not disputed is that many of the leaders of the far right, including David Duke, praised Trump's response, and that a number of business leaders resigned from his advisory councils. Joe Biden later said that the remark was what convinced him to run for president in 2020.

The Shutdown and the Wall

In December 2018 Trump refused to sign a spending bill unless it included five billion, seven hundred million dollars for a wall on the southern border. Congress declined. The government was partially shut down for thirty-five days, from December 22, 2018 to January 25, 2019, the longest in American history at that time, and about eight hundred thousand federal employees went unpaid or were furloughed. Trump ended the shutdown without getting the money. In February 2019 he declared a national emergency at the border to divert funds from military construction to the wall. Congress passed a resolution to terminate the emergency, which he vetoed. Over the course of his term, about four hundred and fifty miles of barrier were built, most of it replacing or reinforcing existing fencing. Mexico did not pay for it.

The Economy

Before the pandemic, the economy grew at a moderate pace, with gross domestic product growth of about two point nine percent in 2018 and two point three in 2019, close to the rates of the last years of the Obama administration. Unemployment fell to three point five percent in early 2020, the lowest in fifty years, and wages, particularly for lower-income workers, rose at a faster clip in 2019. The stock market rose substantially. Supporters credit tax cuts and deregulation. Critics observe that the trend was continuous with the recovery that had begun in 2009, and that the deficit grew even in good times, from about six hundred and sixty-five billion dollars in 2017 to nearly a trillion dollars in 2019. The trade war with China cost American farmers, and the government paid about twenty-eight billion dollars in aid to compensate them. Manufacturing employment grew in 2018 and then stagnated. The economy, in other words, did well by the standards of a long expansion, though it did not do the miraculous things that Trump promised.

COVID-19

In January 2020, as the first cases of a novel coronavirus were identified in the United States, Trump was told by his advisers, including Robert O'Brien, his national security adviser, that it would be the biggest national security threat of his presidency. In February, in a series of interviews for the journalist Bob Woodward that were later published in the book Rage, Trump acknowledged that the virus was deadly, more deadly than even your strenuous flus, and said that he wanted to always play it down. In public, he said that the virus was under control, that it would go away, and that it would disappear like a miracle. He compared it to the flu.

The initial response was hampered by a defective test developed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and by shortages of protective equipment. On March 13 he declared a national emergency, and states began to close businesses and schools. In the following weeks, the White House Coronavirus Task Force, led by Vice President Pence with Dr. Anthony Fauci and Dr. Deborah Birx, held daily briefings. At one such briefing, in April, Trump suggested that researchers look into whether disinfectant could be injected into the body to kill the virus, and that light might be brought inside the body. Medical authorities warned people not to do so. Trump later said that he was being sarcastic. He promoted hydroxychloroquine, a malaria drug, as a treatment; the Food and Drug Administration later revoked its emergency authorization, since studies showed no benefit.

The administration's most successful initiative was Operation Warp Speed, launched in May, which committed billions of dollars to the development and manufacture of vaccines. Two vaccines, from Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, were authorized in December 2020, less than a year after the virus was identified, an extraordinary scientific achievement that supporters credit to the president's decisions. Critics note that the federal role in distributing vaccines, and in messaging on masks and social distancing, had been weak, and that Trump himself disparaged mask-wearing and held large rallies. In October Trump himself was hospitalized with the virus at Walter Reed. By the time he left office about four hundred thousand Americans had died from COVID-19. In total, more than one million would die by 2023. Historians and epidemiologists differ on how much of the death toll can be attributed to federal policy, and how much was unavoidable; some studies suggested that if the United States had had the per-capita death rate of other wealthy countries, hundreds of thousands of deaths might have been avoided.

The Pattern of a Presidency

The first term revealed a consistent pattern. Trump tended to make decisions on the basis of instinct, and to make them fast. He promoted people, and then fired them. During the four years, turnover among his senior staff was greater than in any modern presidency. His chiefs of staff, Reince Priebus, John Kelly and Mick Mulvaney, all left, and he had four national security advisers. He attacked members of his own administration in public, and had a stormy relationship with the press, which he called the enemy of the people.

He also, in his first term, restrained himself from certain courses of action that he was said to have wanted. There was a widespread view among his advisers, later reflected in books like Bob Woodward's Fear and Miles Taylor's anonymous op-ed in the New York Times, that the government had been kept on the rails by officials who quietly refused or delayed his orders. Some of these officials, such as Defense Secretary James Mattis and Chief of Staff Kelly, later spoke out against him. The second term, as we shall see, has been staffed very differently.

The World According to Trump

An Instinct, Not a Doctrine

Every president enters office with a view of the world. Trump's has been hard to summarize, and he has rejected the effort. He does not describe himself as an isolationist or as an interventionist. He says that he is a dealmaker, and that he will take whatever position advances the interests of the United States as he defines them. What can be said with confidence is that he believes that the United States has been exploited by allies and adversaries alike, that trade deficits are losses, that alliances are transactions, and that a president should keep other governments guessing.

Those instincts were evident before he entered politics. In 1987 he spent nearly one hundred thousand dollars on full-page newspaper advertisements calling for the United States to stop paying to defend Japan and other countries that, he said, took advantage of the American taxpayer. The message, which mentioned that the United States was being laughed at around the world, is nearly identical to the one that he was giving audiences thirty years later.

The First Term Abroad

The first term's foreign policy was disrupted by the disputes within the administration, by a stream of departures, and by the president's own unpredictability. Rex Tillerson, the former chief executive of Exxon, was Secretary of State until March 2018, when Trump fired him by tweet, after Tillerson was reported to have called the president a moron. Mike Pompeo replaced him. Michael Flynn lasted twenty-four days as national security adviser and was replaced by Lieutenant General H. R. NATO and Europe. Trump made no secret of his skepticism about NATO, calling it obsolete during the 2016 campaign and later softening the phrase. At the alliance's summit in Brussels in July 2018, he berated the German government over its energy purchases from Russia and demanded that members raise defense spending to four percent of GDP. He wavered on whether the United States would honor Article Five, the mutual defense clause, and reportedly discussed withdrawal. According to later accounts by Bolton and others, he came close. The pressure worked, in a measure: European allies raised their defense budgets, though critics said that they were already on that path. The Europeans, however, were alarmed by the president's attitude, and by his warm relations with authoritarians such as Vladimir Putin of Russia, whom he defended at a summit in Helsinki in July 2018 by appearing to accept Putin's denial of interference in the 2016 election over the conclusions of American intelligence agencies.

China. The most important shift of the first term was toward a harder stance on China. Trump imposed tariffs on some three hundred and sixty billion dollars of Chinese goods beginning in 2018, and China retaliated. The two sides signed a Phase One trade agreement in January 2020, in which China agreed to buy an additional two hundred billion dollars of American goods over two years; it fell well short of that target, in part because of the pandemic. The president later called COVID-19 the China virus and, at times, the Kung Flu, terms that were criticized as fueling hostility toward Asian Americans. In the years since, the view that China is the principal strategic rival of the United States has become the consensus of both parties. Supporters credit Trump with having forced that shift. Critics say that he acted haphazardly and undermined alliances that might have helped to counter China.

North Korea. Trump began his term with threats, saying in August 2017 that North Korea would be met with fire and fury like the world has never seen, and mocking Kim Jong Un as Little Rocket Man. Within a year he had changed course, and in June 2018 he met Kim in Singapore, the first meeting of a sitting American president with a North Korean leader. A second summit in Hanoi in February 2019 broke down over sanctions. In June 2019, he stepped briefly across the line into North Korea at the demilitarized zone. There was no agreement on the dismantling of the North's nuclear weapons, and its arsenal continued to grow. Trump has said, on many occasions, that he and Kim fell in love. Critics said that he gave a brutal dictator the legitimacy of a summit in exchange for nothing.

Iran's response included attacks on shipping and on Saudi oil facilities, and in June 2019 it shot down an American drone. Trump called off a retaliatory strike at the last minute. In January 2020, he ordered a drone strike in Baghdad that killed General Qassem Soleimani, the head of Iran's Quds Force, and Iran responded with missile strikes on bases in Iraq, causing brain injuries in more than a hundred American service members but no deaths. Afghanistan. In February 2020, the Trump administration signed an agreement with the Taliban in Doha, under which the United States agreed to withdraw all its forces by May 2021 in exchange for the Taliban's promise not to allow terrorist groups to operate from Afghanistan. No aspect of Trump's foreign policy has generated more argument than his approach to Russia. In the first term, he was repeatedly accused of being too accommodating to Putin. The Second Term: A More Assertive Foreign Policy

The foreign policy of the second term has been more assertive and more personal than that of the first. The main events are described in earlier chapters, but the shape deserves a summary. The president has used the threat of tariffs as an instrument to achieve aims that have nothing to do with trade, including immigration and the prosecution of Brazil's former president. He has spoken openly of acquiring Greenland and of taking control of the Panama Canal, and has said that Canada should become the fifty-first state, a proposal that infuriated Canadians and was widely treated in that country as an insult. He has withdrawn the United States from the World Health Organization and cut foreign aid sharply.

He has also, in the second term, used military force with fewer of the reservations that marked the first: against Iran's nuclear sites in June 2025, against vessels in the Caribbean, in the capture of President Maduro in January 2026, and in the war with Iran that began in February. The change has been noted by his supporters, who see a president who is finally willing to act, and by his critics, who see a president whose impulses are no longer restrained by aides who might counsel caution. The costs have been substantial. The war with Iran is one of the largest American military engagements since the Iraq war, and the economic effects have been felt at gas stations across the country.

Assessment

The evidence in this chapter suggests a president whose foreign policy has been more consistent than his style. He has consistently favored bilateral deals over multilateral commitments, the use of economic coercion over diplomacy, and personal relationships with strong leaders over institutional ties. He has been consistently skeptical of alliances and of foreign aid. And he has been consistently unwilling to describe the promotion of democracy or human rights as an aim of American policy.

Whether this approach has served American interests is a matter on which scholars and practitioners disagree. There are real achievements on the record, above all the Abraham Accords and the shift on China. There are also real costs: strained alliances, an unresolved war in Europe, an unresolved war in the Middle East, and a reputation for unreliability that adversaries and friends alike have noted. The verdict will depend, in large part, on how the wars that are under way now end.

Chapter 13
The Language and the Press

The Talker

No modern politician has been as much a creature of his own voice as Donald Trump. Before he ran for anything, he was on the radio with Howard Stern, on television as a game-show host, and in print as a source for gossip columnists. His campaigns were conducted largely on stage, before crowds that ran to twenty thousand, in speeches that ran to ninety minutes and were rarely read from a script. In an age in which most candidates work with teams of speechwriters and consultants, he has always preferred to speak for himself.

His style has been analyzed by linguists, political scientists and comedians. Common to most accounts are the following features. He speaks in short sentences and simple words. Analyses of transcripts by researchers at Carnegie Mellon and others found that his vocabulary was, by conventional readability measures, at about a middle-school level or below, lower than that of recent presidents, and his supporters regard this as a virtue: he speaks the way that ordinary people speak. He uses superlatives, calling things the greatest, the worst, the biggest, the best ever seen. He repeats. He makes a point, digresses, returns to it, and repeats it. He tells stories, often exaggerated, about people he has met, and often refers to unnamed authorities: many people are saying, everybody knows, believe me. He uses nicknames, which he applies to opponents with remarkable consistency and effect.

The nicknames are among his most effective techniques. Crooked Hillary, Lyin' Ted, Low Energy Jeb, Little Marco, Sleepy Joe, Shifty Schiff, Cryin' Chuck, and Pocahontas, for Senator Elizabeth Warren, each condensed an attack into a phrase that could be repeated by supporters and picked up by the media. Some were unfair; some were effective; some were widely criticized as offensive, notably the last of these, which many Native Americans found insulting. Their success can be measured in the way that opponents came to be defined by them, and in the way that they were repeated by people who never intended to endorse them.

Twitter

The instrument through which the style became a political weapon was Twitter. Trump joined the platform in March 2009 and by the time he entered the White House had more than twenty million followers. He wrote many of the messages himself, often in the early morning, in capital letters and with exclamation marks. Through the medium he announced policies, attacked opponents, fired officials and, on occasion, contradicted his own aides. The president's tweets moved markets and dominated the news cycle. In the first term, according to archives, he posted more than twenty-five thousand times.

The messages served several purposes. They set the agenda of the news media, which felt compelled to cover them, and had the effect that Trump had understood since the 1980s, of keeping him at the center of the story. They allowed him to speak directly to his supporters without the filter of the press. And they gave those supporters the sense that they were hearing from the man himself. The critics said that the tweets were often false, often cruel, and sometimes dangerous, as when he attacked private individuals, or when, on January 6, 2021, he tweeted an attack on his vice president while the Capitol was being overrun.

On January 8, 2021, two days after the attack, Twitter permanently suspended his account, citing the risk of further incitement of violence. Facebook and YouTube suspended him as well. For nearly two years he was without the platform that had been his principal means of communication. He launched a new social network, Truth Social, in February 2022, which never attracted a large audience compared with Twitter. In November 2022, after Elon Musk bought Twitter, renamed it X, and restored Trump's account, Trump did not immediately return, preferring to use Truth Social, but he resumed posting on X in 2024, in the course of his presidential campaign, and it remained one of his tools in the second term.

Fake News

The other innovation was the systematic attack on the press. Trump did not invent hostility toward journalists, which is almost as old as the republic. But he elevated it to a defining principle of his political identity. From 2015 onward, he referred to media organizations he disliked as fake news, a phrase that until then had described fabricated stories spread on the internet. In February 2017, a month after the inauguration, he tweeted that the failing New York Times, NBC News, ABC, CBS and CNN were the enemy of the American People. The phrase has a history in totalitarian regimes, and press freedom groups warned against it. He never withdrew it.

The attack served purposes. It gave his supporters a reason to discount unfavorable stories, whatever their source. It gave him an all-purpose reply to accusations. And, according to some scholars, it worked because his supporters already distrusted the press, and because polls showed that public confidence in the media had fallen over decades. The Gallup Organization found in 2024 that trust in the mass media had reached the lowest level in the history of its polling.

At the same time, Trump has had a complicated relationship with the media he attacks. He is a compulsive consumer of television news, and by many accounts calls reporters himself. He has granted interviews to reporters from organizations that he denounces, including the New York Times, from which he has cultivated a reputation as a source. His favorite network, Fox News, was for years a supporter, though it provided him with plenty of frustration, as when, on election night in 2020, it was the first to call Arizona for Biden. The network's hosts, as we have seen, privately doubted his claims of fraud, and the disclosures in the Dominion lawsuit angered him.

In the second term, the president has used the legal system and the government's power against media organizations in ways that have no precedent in modern times. A number of media companies have settled with him. In December 2024, ABC News paid fifteen million dollars to his presidential library to settle a defamation suit over statements by the host George Stephanopoulos, who had said that a jury had found Trump liable for rape. Critics regard these settlements as a form of tribute paid by companies with business before the government to a president who could affect them. The companies deny that the settlements were connected to their regulatory interests. Trump has also sued the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, and has threatened other outlets, and there have been reports that a number of the suits have been dismissed or narrowed by the courts.

The administration has also acted more directly. The Pentagon adopted rules limiting the access of reporters, and many major organizations refused to sign them and turned in their credentials. In September 2026, according to news reports, Trump announced a ban on reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The three outlets sued, and a federal judge blocked the ban and restored their access.

Truth and Consequences

The most serious charge against Trump's use of language is that it has degraded the public's ability to distinguish between true and false statements, and that it has done so deliberately. He has said that he is a counterpuncher, that he responds to what is said about him, and that his exaggerations are a form of showmanship. The phrase truthful hyperbole was used by his ghostwriter Tony Schwartz. Critics say that the difference between hyperbole and lying is the difference between statements that are obviously not meant to be taken literally and those that are meant to be believed; and that many of the claims that he made, about crowd sizes, about the election, about the number of people who died in Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, about the effects of his policies, were of the latter kind.

His defenders take a different view. They repeat the observation of the journalist Salena Zito in 2016, that the press takes him literally but not seriously, while his supporters take him seriously but not literally. They say that reporters seize on isolated remarks and treat them as significant, while ignoring the substance. They argue that other politicians shade the truth, and that the press applies a double standard, more forgiving of Democrats. And they note that the same media that condemned him for falsehoods carried false claims about him, as in the Russia investigation and the story of the bounty on American troops in Afghanistan.

Both positions capture something. What is beyond question is that Trump's rhetoric has changed the way in which Americans talk about politics. The vocabulary of fake news, enemy of the people, witch hunt and rigged election has entered common speech. His style has been adopted by many politicians in both parties, and the incentives that reward attention over accuracy, which he exploited so well, show no sign of weakening. That effect may prove more lasting than any policy that he enacted.
