The 2016 Campaign

The campaign brought the issues to the center of American politics. At the opening in June 2015, his remarks that some Mexican immigrants were rapists and criminals were denounced by many Republicans and by business partners, and, as a matter of fact, defended by others. His proposal in December 2015 for a shutdown of Muslim immigration was the subject of national debate. In February 2016, asked by an interviewer whether he would disavow the endorsement of David Duke, the former Ku Klux Klan leader, Trump said that he did not know anything about him, though he had disavowed him earlier, and blamed a faulty earpiece. In June of that year, he asserted that Judge Gonzalo Curiel could not be fair to him because he was of Mexican heritage, though Curiel was born in Indiana. House Speaker Paul Ryan called it a textbook example of a racist comment.

Defenders of Trump said then, and say now, that the remarks about Mexican rapists referred to criminals, not to all Mexicans, and that the proposals on immigration and terrorism were matters of security. They add that he attracted a substantial number of votes from Hispanic and Black Americans, and that, in 2024, he did better among these groups than any Republican in decades. Critics respond that a politician can attract votes from members of a minority group and still stoke hostility toward it, and that Trump's rhetoric, particularly on immigration, has repeatedly gone beyond policy.

The First Term

Some of the most contentious incidents occurred during the first term. The response to Charlottesville, described in Chapter Eleven, drew the condemnation of a number of Republican leaders. In January 2018, in a meeting on immigration, Trump was reported by several people present to have asked why the United States accepted immigrants from what he called shithole countries, in reference to Haiti and African nations, and to have said that the country should take more people from Norway. He denied having used the word, though one senator present, Dick Durbin, said that he had. In July 2019, he wrote on Twitter that four Democratic congresswomen of color, three of whom were born in the United States, should go back and fix the totally broken and crime infested places from which they came. The House condemned the remarks in a resolution; four Republicans voted with the Democrats.

Among the accomplishments that supporters cite on the same topic are the First Step Act, criminal justice reform signed in December 2018, which reduced mandatory minimum sentences and allowed the release of thousands of federal prisoners, disproportionately Black. They cite the funding for historically Black colleges and universities, the creation of opportunity zones, and the record low unemployment among Black and Hispanic workers before the pandemic. Critics say that these measures were modest, compared with the harm that they attribute to his rhetoric, his approach to policing, and his opposition to the Black Lives Matter protests of 2020, which he called symbols of hate and which he met with threats of military force. In June 2020, federal officers used tear gas to clear peaceful protesters from Lafayette Square in front of the White House shortly before he walked across the park to be photographed holding a Bible in front of St. John's Church. The clearance, which he said was unrelated, was described by the Park Police as having been planned earlier; an inspector general found that the officers had not cleared the park for the photo, and that the decision predated the president's plans, though the timing was widely criticized.

Immigration and Nationalism

His deeper political position is a form of nationalism. He believes that the United States should put its own citizens first in trade, immigration and foreign policy, that borders should be enforced, and that cultural cohesion matters. In the 2016 campaign and afterwards, he used the word globalist, sometimes as an insult, which critics saw as a coded reference to Jews; he has said that the term has nothing to do with religion. He has claimed that immigrants are poisoning the blood of the country, a phrase used in December 2023, which critics compared to Nazi rhetoric and which his aides said was not meant in a racial sense. In the 2024 campaign, he told voters that migrants were coming from prisons and insane asylums, and repeated the claim, refuted by local officials, that Haitian migrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating pets.

The immigration policies of the second term have been the most aggressive of any modern president, as described in Chapter Twenty-two. Supporters say that enforcement of the laws is a basic function of government, that the previous administration allowed the system to break down, and that the public voted for a crackdown. Critics say that agents have detained and deported people with no criminal record, including in some cases American citizens, that a number of children have been affected, that the government has used force against peaceful protesters, and that the rhetoric surrounding the policy has dehumanized immigrants as a class.

The most significant legal question concerns the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of citizenship to those born in the United States. In January 2025, the president signed an order to end birthright citizenship for the children of people in the country illegally or temporarily. Lower courts blocked it, and the Supreme Court took up the question of the scope of those injunctions and the merits. Most scholars of constitutional law consider the order to contradict the text of the amendment and the Court's precedent, going back to an 1898 decision. Supporters argue that the phrase subject to the jurisdiction thereof was not intended to cover the children of people who are in the country unlawfully.

Antisemitism and Its Uses

An especially delicate area concerns antisemitism. Trump has been a strong supporter of Israel, has Jewish family members, and has appointed Jewish officials to senior posts. He has also been accused of antisemitic tropes: in 2015 he told the Republican Jewish Coalition that they would not support him because he did not want their money, and in 2019 he said that Jewish Democrats who voted for their party were disloyal, a remark that Jewish organizations, including some allied with him, criticized. In November 2022, he hosted at Mar-a-Lago dinner guests including the rapper Ye, who had made antisemitic statements, and Nick Fuentes, a white nationalist, whom Trump said he did not know. In the aftermath of the October 7, 2023 attack, his administration cracked down on pro-Palestinian protests at universities, which supporters described as a response to antisemitism on campus and critics as an attack on free speech, and in some cases involved the detention and attempted deportation of foreign students for their speech. The record of the second term includes a range of measures against universities, including the withholding of federal funding from Harvard and Columbia, which are still being contested in the courts.

Assessment

On the question of Trump's motives, the honest answer is that they cannot be known. The record establishes that he has said things that many Americans, including many of his supporters, regard as offensive, and that he has made appeals to fear of immigrants and of minorities that were unusual for a president. It also establishes that he has attracted substantial support from minority voters, that some of his policies were intended to help them, and that he rejects the label of racist.

The most defensible reading might be that Trump treats identity as a tool of politics, and is neither committed to racial hierarchy nor concerned by the effect of his words on the groups that he targets. But a fair account must also give weight to those who think that this is too generous, and who argue that the effect of the words is the same regardless of the intent. It should also note that many of his supporters do not experience his rhetoric as racist, and that the disagreement about it has become one of the deepest divisions in American life. That division will outlast him.

Chapter 15
Two Impeachments

The Call

On the morning of July 25, 2019, the day after Robert Mueller's testimony to Congress, President Trump placed a phone call to the newly elected president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky. The call lasted about thirty minutes. A rough transcript, released by the White House in September, records Zelensky thanking Trump for American support and saying that his country was almost ready to buy more Javelin anti-tank missiles from the United States. Trump replied, I would like you to do us a favor though.

The favor, as recorded in the transcript, concerned two matters. One was a theory that Ukraine, and not Russia, had interfered in the 2016 election, involving a server belonging to the Democratic National Committee. The other was a request that Zelensky look into Joe Biden and his son, Hunter Biden, who had joined the board of a Ukrainian gas company, Burisma, in 2014, when his father was vice president. Trump said that there were reports that Biden had stopped the prosecution of a corrupt prosecutor, and asked Zelensky to look into it. He urged him to talk to Attorney General Barr and to his personal lawyer, Rudy Giuliani.

The context mattered. Days before the call, the White House had frozen almost four hundred million dollars in military aid that Congress had appropriated for Ukraine, which was engaged in a war with Russian-backed separatists. The freeze was not disclosed to the Ukrainian government until later, but it had been discussed inside the administration, and career officials had expressed alarm. Zelensky had also been seeking a meeting in the White House, which was withheld.

The Whistleblower

A member of the intelligence community, who was later identified in press reports but remained protected under law, filed a complaint with the intelligence community's inspector general on August 12, alleging that the president had used the power of his office to solicit interference from a foreign country in the 2020 election. The inspector general found the complaint credible and urgent. The acting Director of National Intelligence, Joseph Maguire, initially refused to send it to Congress, on the advice of the Justice Department. In September, after reporting in the Washington Post and a rebellion in Congress, the complaint was released. The aid to Ukraine was released on September 11, without explanation, a few days after Congress had begun investigating.

On September 24 Speaker Nancy Pelosi announced a formal impeachment inquiry. In a series of depositions and public hearings led by the House Intelligence Committee under Adam Schiff, a parade of diplomats and career officials testified about the pressure that had been placed on Ukraine. The ambassador to the European Union, Gordon Sondland, a Trump donor, testified that there had been a quid pro quo: that a White House meeting had been conditioned on a public announcement of investigations. Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Vindman, who had listened to the call, testified that he thought the request was improper. Ambassador William Taylor testified that it was crazy to withhold security assistance for help with a domestic political campaign. Fiona Hill, a former Russia analyst on the National Security Council, warned against what she called a fictional narrative that Ukraine had interfered in the election. Marie Yovanovitch, the former ambassador to Ukraine, who had been recalled after a smear campaign led by Giuliani, gave emotional testimony.

Trump denied that there was any quid pro quo, called the call perfect, and instructed the administration to defy subpoenas. The White House refused to provide witnesses or documents. Republican members of Congress argued that the aid was ultimately released, that Zelensky had said that he felt no pressure, and that the process was a partisan sham. Some also argued that the request to investigate the Bidens was a legitimate concern about corruption.

The First Impeachment

On December 18, 2019, the House of Representatives voted, largely along party lines, to impeach Trump on two articles: abuse of power, by a vote of 230 to 197, and obstruction of Congress, by 229 to 198. He became the third president to be impeached, after Andrew Johnson and Bill Clinton. Pelosi delayed sending the articles to the Senate for several weeks.

The trial in the Senate began in January 2020. The prosecution, led by seven House managers, argued that Trump had used the powers of his office for personal gain and had then obstructed the inquiry. Trump's defense team, which included the attorneys Pat Cipollone, Jay Sekulow and, at times, Alan Dershowitz, argued that the impeachment was a partisan attack and that there had been no crime. Dershowitz argued that a president could not be impeached for actions that he believed were in the public interest, on the theory that he would have done what was necessary to be reelected. In one of the sharpest disputes, the Senate voted 51 to 49 not to call witnesses, after a bombshell report that John Bolton, the former national security adviser, had written in a draft of his forthcoming book that Trump had told him that he wanted to withhold the aid until Ukraine helped with investigations of the Democrats. Bolton later published the book.

On February 5, 2020, the Senate acquitted Trump on both counts. The vote on abuse of power was 52 to 48, and on obstruction, 53 to 47. Conviction required sixty-seven votes. One Republican, Senator Mitt Romney of Utah, voted to convict on the first article, becoming the first senator in history to vote to convict a president of his own party. Trump celebrated the result with a speech in the East Room in which he called his opponents evil and vicious. In the weeks that followed, he fired Vindman and Sondland, and Inspector General Michael Atkinson, who had handled the whistleblower complaint.

The Lesson

What Trump drew from the first impeachment was perhaps the most consequential thing that came out of it. He had been accused of using the power of the government to pressure a foreign power to help him win an election. He had been shown, by the evidence, to have done something like it. And nothing had happened. The Republican senators, with one exception, had decided that whatever he had done did not merit removal, and the public, in the polls, was divided along the same lines as before.

The lesson, as most scholars of the presidency and many of his critics have concluded, was that the institutional checks on a president were weaker than had been thought. If Congress was unwilling to remove a president who acted in a partisan way, then the only real check was the election. Trump's later behavior, in 2020 and thereafter, seems consistent with the conclusion that he had learned this. He was later to say, about the events that led to his second impeachment, that he had done nothing wrong, and, about the prosecutions, that they were the continuation of the effort to destroy him.

The Second Impeachment

The second impeachment arrived within days of the end of his term, in the aftermath of the assault on the Capitol. The events of January 6, 2021, are described in Chapter Seventeen, and it is enough here to record the political sequence. On January 11, the House Democrats introduced a single article of impeachment charging Trump with incitement of insurrection. On January 13, the House voted 232 to 197 to impeach him, with ten Republicans joining the Democrats. It was the most bipartisan impeachment vote in American history, and Trump was the first president to be impeached twice.

The Senate trial began on February 9, after Trump had left office, raising a constitutional question about whether a former president could be tried. The Senate voted that it could. The House managers, led by Representative Jamie Raskin, presented a case built on video of the riot and on Trump's own statements, and argued that the president had spent months preparing his supporters for a violent confrontation over the election. Trump's lawyers, Bruce Castor and David Schoen, argued that the trial was unconstitutional, that his speech was protected by the First Amendment, and that he had not intended violence.

On February 13, the Senate voted 57 to 43 to convict, ten short of two-thirds. Seven Republicans joined the Democrats. Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell voted to acquit, on the ground that the Senate lacked jurisdiction over a former president, but then delivered a speech on the Senate floor in which he said that there was no question that Trump was practically and morally responsible for provoking the events of the day. He added that a former president was not immune from criminal or civil accountability. That sentence was to be quoted often over the years that followed.

The Balance Sheet

The two impeachments produced no conviction, and, unlike the impeachment of Richard Nixon, which was headed off by his resignation, they did not end a presidency. They did produce a record: of a president who was found by the House on two occasions to have committed acts of such gravity that he should be removed, and who was twice acquitted by a Senate whose members were divided by party. Defenders of the president consider the impeachments to have been partisan efforts, brought by a party that had opposed him since his election, and argue that the Senate verdicts vindicated him. Critics regard the acquittals as evidence that the Senate had abdicated its responsibility.

Both views have an element of truth. The impeachments did fail. But they left a mark that the president never forgave. In his second term he has sought retribution, in the courts, in the administration and in public, against many of the officials who took part. Vindman, and his brother, were among the first to be removed from their posts, and, in his second term, Trump revoked security clearances for critics and ordered investigations into some of his former officials. Whether or not this is a matter of justice, it is a matter of record that the president has pursued it.

Chapter 16
The Loss

Before the Votes Were Counted

The most consequential decision Donald Trump made about the 2020 election was made months before it was held. Beginning in the spring, as states expanded voting by mail because of the pandemic, he said repeatedly that mail voting would produce the most fraudulent election in history. He said the election would be rigged. Asked in July on Fox News whether he would accept the results, he said that he would have to see. He told a rally in September that the only way they could take this election away from us is if this is a rigged election. Asked in a debate whether he would commit to a peaceful transfer of power, he said that we're going to have to see what happens.

The reasons that Trump gave for his claims were not supported by evidence. Election officials in both parties, as well as academic studies over many years, had found that fraud in mail voting was rare. But the claim had a political logic. Polls showed that Democrats were much more likely than Republicans to vote by mail, and that as a result the early counts on election night were likely to favor Trump, and the later counts, which included mail ballots, were likely to favor Biden. This pattern, which was predicted in advance by election analysts, came to be known as the red mirage. Trump's advisers, including some in his campaign, understood it. The president, on the evidence of what he said on election night, planned to use it.

Election Night

On the night of November 3, Trump led in several states, including Florida, Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, and at about two-thirty in the morning he went to the East Room of the White House and declared that we were winning, and that this was a fraud on the American public. He said that we want all voting to stop. He added that he would go to the Supreme Court.

But the votes were not finished. As mail ballots were counted over the following days, the leads in Pennsylvania, Georgia, Michigan, Wisconsin and Arizona shifted to Biden. On November 7, the networks called Pennsylvania, and with it the election, for Biden. In the final tally, Biden won 306 electoral votes to Trump's 232, the reverse of Trump's own pledged margin in 2016. He won the popular vote by more than seven million votes, or about four and a half percentage points. The margins in the decisive states were narrow: about twelve thousand votes in Georgia, ten thousand in Arizona, and about twenty thousand in Wisconsin. Had about forty-three thousand more votes in those three states gone to Trump, the Electoral College would have been tied and the House of Representatives would have chosen the president.

Trump did not concede. He said that he had won, and that the election had been stolen. That claim would be repeated for years, and it is the most important political fact of the first half of the 2020s.

The Lawsuits

Between November 3 and December, Trump and his allies filed more than sixty lawsuits in state and federal courts challenging the results. They lost almost all of them. In some, the judges, including many appointed by Trump, dismissed the cases for lack of standing or evidence. In others they ruled on the merits. In Pennsylvania, a federal judge, Matthew Brann, a Republican and a member of the Federalist Society, wrote in an opinion that the Trump campaign had presented strained legal arguments without merit and speculative accusations, unpled in the complaint and unsupported by evidence. The Third Circuit, in an opinion written by Judge Stephanos Bibas, a Trump appointee, wrote that charges of unfairness are serious, but calling an election unfair does not make it so, and that charges require specific allegations and then proof.

In December the Supreme Court declined to hear a suit brought by the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, that asked it to invalidate the results in four states that Biden had won. The suit was supported by more than one hundred Republican members of the House of Representatives and by seventeen Republican state attorneys general. The Court said that Texas had not shown a judicially cognizable interest in how another state conducts its elections. Trump's own attorney general, William Barr, said on December 1 that the Department of Justice had not seen fraud on a scale that could have affected a different outcome in the election. Trump's director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Christopher Krebs, who had said that the election was the most secure in American history, was fired by tweet.

The most publicized element of the effort was a series of press conferences by Trump's private attorney, the former New York City mayor Rudy Giuliani, and by lawyers such as Sidney Powell and Jenna Ellis. Powell said that the election was stolen through a scheme, run by Venezuelan officials, involving Dominion Voting Systems machines. In a famous press conference at the Republican National Committee's offices on November 19, Giuliani said that there had been a massive fraud, though a few moments later a trickle of hair dye ran down his face. In court, when asked whether he was alleging fraud, Giuliani said that he was not. A judge in Pennsylvania noted that the campaign's filing did not allege fraud.

The claims that were made on television had legal consequences of their own. Dominion sued Fox News, Giuliani, Powell and others for defamation, and in April 2023, on the eve of the trial, Fox agreed to pay eight hundred and thirty-seven and a half million dollars to settle the case. In discovery, it had emerged that Fox hosts and executives had privately doubted or dismissed the claims about the election that they were broadcasting. In 2023, Giuliani, Ellis and Powell were among the co-defendants in a criminal indictment in Georgia. In December 2023, a federal jury in Washington awarded one hundred and forty-eight million dollars in damages to two Georgia election workers, Ruby Freeman and her daughter Wandrea Moss, whom Giuliani had falsely accused of manipulating ballots. In 2024 Giuliani was disbarred in New York, and he filed for bankruptcy.

The Georgia Call

On January 2, 2021, Trump telephoned the Georgia Secretary of State, Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, and spent about an hour urging him to change the state's result. A recording of the call was published by the Washington Post. Trump told Raffensperger that he wanted him to find eleven thousand, seven hundred and eighty votes, which was one more than the margin by which he had lost the state. He said that there was nothing wrong with saying that you recalculated. He alleged that hundreds of thousands of ballots had been fraudulently cast, claims that Raffensperger's staff rebutted with data. At one point Trump said that it was a criminal offense if Raffensperger and his lawyer did not act, and that it was a big risk to them.

Trump has said that the call was perfect. His lawyers argued that he was merely raising concerns that he believed to be true. The Fulton County District Attorney, Fani Willis, opened a criminal investigation, and it is discussed in Chapter Eighteen.

The Pressure on the Vice President

The last constitutional step in the process was the counting of electoral votes by Congress on January 6, presided over by the vice president, Mike Pence. The Electoral Count Act of 1887 gave the vice president a ministerial role: to open the certificates and to count them. But in December a lawyer named John Eastman, a law professor who had clerked for Justice Clarence Thomas, wrote a memo arguing that the vice president had the power to reject electors from states in dispute or to delay the count and send the matter back to the state legislatures. Trump seized on the idea. He said in public that Pence had the power to overturn the election, and told him in private, in phone calls and meetings, that he should do so.

Pence, who consulted with lawyers, former Vice President Dan Quayle and Senate parliamentarians, concluded that he did not have the power to do so. He told Trump in a meeting on January 4 that he could not. Trump told him that he would be a wimp if he did not act, and, according to testimony later given to the House committee, was angrier still on the morning of January 6, when he called Pence again. On the morning of January 6, Trump tweeted that if Pence did the right thing, we win the election. Pence did not.

What the Claim Was

It is important to be specific about what the claim of a stolen election was and what evidence supported it. The claim asserted that millions of votes had been cast illegally or miscounted, and that these had made the difference. The evidence for this proposition was examined in dozens of court cases, in recounts and audits, including a hand recount in Georgia and a review by a Republican-led firm in Arizona, and in investigations by state officials and by the Trump Justice Department. Each of them confirmed the original result. In the Arizona review, by a firm called Cyber Ninjas, the count of Maricopa County ballots came out with Biden slightly ahead by a bigger margin than in the official count. A group of Republican former officials and lawyers, including the conservative judge J. Michael Luttig, said that the claim was baseless.

Some of Trump's claims turned out to concern real irregularities. There were isolated instances of voter fraud in 2020, as in every election, involving a few dozen people, and some of them were Trump supporters. Some states had changed their voting rules during the pandemic through means that some legal scholars believed to be unlawful. But none of these approached the scale needed to alter a result, and none of them was found to have done so.

The question that would occupy the courts, the Congress and the voters for the next four years was not whether Trump was mistaken about the election, but whether he knew it, and what he did about it. On that question, his own advisers gave evidence. Barr said he told Trump that the claims were bullshit. Trump's campaign manager Bill Stepien and his campaign's own data analyst told him that he had lost. Trump's White House lawyers told him that there was no basis to overturn the results. According to the testimony gathered by the House Select Committee, and by the special counsel Jack Smith, Trump was informed repeatedly and by many of his most trusted advisers that the claims were false. He continued to make them. The consequences of that decision came on January 6.

January 6

The Rally

On the morning of Wednesday, January 6, 2021, tens of thousands of people gathered on the Ellipse, south of the White House, for a rally called Save America. Trump had promoted it in December with a tweet, saying that there would be a big protest in D.C. on January 6th, and adding: Be there, will be wild! Many of the people who came believed, on the strength of his statements, that the election had been stolen and that Congress and the vice president could still reverse it.

The Secret Service and the organizers had scanned attendees with magnetometers, and had confiscated a large number of weapons, including knives, pepper spray, brass knuckles, stun guns and body armor. According to testimony to the House Select Committee, Trump was told this, and was told that many in the crowd were armed, and that they did not want to go through the magnetometers because they did not want their weapons taken. He said, according to a former White House aide, Cassidy Hutchinson, who testified about what she had heard and been told, that he did not care that they had weapons, because they were not there to hurt him, and that they should be allowed to go to the Capitol. He also asked that the magnetometers be taken away. Trump has denied the account, and other witnesses gave more limited versions.

Trump spoke at about noon. His speech lasted more than an hour. He repeated the claims about the stolen election. He said that we won this election, and we won it by a landslide. He said that Pence needed to do the right thing. He said: if you don't fight like hell you're not going to have a country anymore. He said that we're going to walk down to the Capitol, and that we're going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women. He added that he did not think that we're going to be cheering so much for some of them. In the speech he said that they should peacefully and patriotically make their voices heard. He said that he would be with them. He did not walk to the Capitol; he returned to the White House.

The Attack

At about one o'clock, as the joint session of Congress began to count the electoral votes, thousands of people moved toward the Capitol. Some had heard Trump; others had not been at the rally at all. Among them were organized groups, including members of the Proud Boys and the Oath Keepers, who had made plans for the day. At about 12:53 the crowd began to breach the outer barricades. Officers of the Capitol Police and the Metropolitan Police, who were outnumbered, were attacked with flagpoles, bear spray, chemical irritants and fists. The mob broke windows, entered the building, and, at about two-fourteen, forced its way into the Senate chamber, moments after senators had been evacuated. Vice President Pence, who was at the Capitol, was taken to a secure location. Rioters chanted Hang Mike Pence, and a gallows was erected outside.

About a hundred and forty police officers were injured, and at least some of them suffered serious injuries including brain damage and broken bones. Officer Brian Sicknick, who had been sprayed with a chemical irritant during the fighting, died the following day; the medical examiner ruled that he had died of natural causes, two strokes, but said that all that transpired played a role in his condition. Ashli Babbitt, a rioter, was shot dead by a Capitol Police officer as she tried to climb through a broken window into the Speaker's Lobby. Three other people died of medical emergencies at the scene. In the following days and months, four police officers who had defended the Capitol died by suicide.

Three Hours

From about one o'clock, as the attack began, Trump was in the private dining room off the Oval Office, watching the events on television. Over the next three hours, according to the evidence gathered by the House Select Committee, he received many entreaties to call off the crowd. His daughter Ivanka Trump, his chief of staff Mark Meadows, his lawyer Pat Cipollone, and his allies including Fox News hosts and Republican members of Congress urged him to act. Kevin McCarthy, the House Republican leader, called him and, according to McCarthy's later account and to statements by Representative Jaime Herrera Beutler, said that the rioters were his supporters, and that he had to get them to stop. Trump, according to Herrera Beutler, told McCarthy that the people were more upset about the election than McCarthy was.

At 2:24 p.m., he tweeted that Mike Pence didn't have the courage to do what should have been done to protect our Country and our Constitution. At 2:38, he tweeted that everyone should stay peaceful. At 3:13, he tweeted again to stay peaceful. At 4:17, he released a video in which he told the rioters that we love you, you're very special, and that they should go home in peace, but repeated that the election was stolen. In the evening he tweeted that these are the things and events that happen when a sacred landslide election victory is so unceremoniously and viciously stripped away.

The House Select Committee, chaired by Representative Bennie Thompson and with two Republican members, Liz Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, concluded that the president had for three hours failed to act, and that this was a dereliction of duty. It found that he had not called the military or law enforcement, had not ordered the National Guard to the Capitol, and had not made a public statement telling the rioters to leave until more than three hours after the attack began. The White House says that he had been focused on the security of the Capitol. The committee's account has been challenged by Republicans, who called the investigation partisan, and who noted that the Republican leader had withdrawn his nominees to the committee after the Speaker rejected two of them.

The Aftermath

By nine that evening, the Capitol had been cleared, and Congress resumed its work. At about 3:40 the next morning, it completed the count and declared Joseph Biden the winner. Trump released a statement through an aide that there would be an orderly transition. In the days that followed, a number of cabinet officials resigned, including Secretary of Education Betsy DeVos and Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao. Twitter, Facebook and other social media companies suspended his accounts.

The Department of Justice began one of the largest investigations in its history. Over the next four years, more than fourteen hundred people were charged with crimes related to January 6, including assaulting police officers, seditious conspiracy, obstruction of an official proceeding, and trespassing. Enrique Tarrio of the Proud Boys was convicted of seditious conspiracy and sentenced to twenty-two years in prison. Stewart Rhodes, the leader of the Oath Keepers, was convicted of seditious conspiracy and sentenced to eighteen years. The great majority of defendants pleaded guilty, and most received sentences of less than a year. Some of the most serious were prosecuted for violent attacks on police, and a number of them received sentences of ten years or more.

The Committee and the Special Counsel

The House Select Committee held ten public hearings in the summer and fall of 2022, and issued a final report in December. It concluded that Trump had, over a period of months, laid the groundwork for the attack by spreading false claims of election fraud, had pressured state officials, the Justice Department and the vice president to overturn the election, and had summoned the crowd and then failed to stop the attack. It recommended that the Department of Justice consider criminal charges against Trump for obstructing an official proceeding, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to make a false statement, and inciting or assisting an insurrection.

On November 18, 2022, three days after Trump announced his candidacy for a second term, Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed Jack Smith, a career prosecutor who had headed the war crimes unit at The Hague, as special counsel to oversee the investigations of the events of January 6 and of the classified documents at Mar-a-Lago. In August 2023, Smith's grand jury indicted Trump on four counts: conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to obstruct an official proceeding, obstruction of an official proceeding, and conspiracy against rights. The indictment alleged that the president had spread knowingly false claims to overturn the results, and that he had done so in the pursuit of power. It did not charge insurrection.

Trump pleaded not guilty. His lawyers argued that his actions were within the scope of his official duties and that he was immune from prosecution, and that the prosecution violated his right to free speech. The trial was set for March 2024, but it never took place. In July 2024, in Trump v. United States, the Supreme Court held, by six to three, that a president has absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for actions within his core constitutional powers, and presumptive immunity for other official acts, and that the president cannot be prosecuted on the basis of official acts, even to prove the character of unofficial ones. The decision sent the case back to the trial judge, Tanya Chutkan, to determine which acts were official. It was a victory for Trump, and it delayed the case beyond the election. After Trump was elected in November 2024, Smith moved to dismiss the case, on the ground that Justice Department policy prohibited the prosecution of a sitting president. The judge granted the request.

The Pardons

On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump issued pardons or commutations to about fifteen hundred people who had been convicted or charged in connection with January 6. The clemency covered those who had been convicted of assaulting police officers. It also freed those who had been convicted of seditious conspiracy, including Tarrio, who was pardoned, and Rhodes, whose sentence was commuted. Trump said that he was granting pardons to hostages. Vice President Vance said that people who had committed violence against police should not have been pardoned, although he, too, had said in earlier statements that he supported clemency for many of those who had been prosecuted. In the following months several of the pardoned people were arrested on new charges, including weapons and domestic violence charges. The Capitol Police union protested the pardons.

What January 6 Meant

There is no dispute about the basic facts. A crowd, mobilized by a president who claimed that an election had been stolen, attacked the Capitol during the counting of electoral votes, and the counting was delayed for hours. Beyond these facts, disagreements begin. Trump and his supporters say that the crowd was a spontaneous eruption, that most of the participants were peaceful, that the president had told them to protest peacefully, that the Capitol Police had been unprepared, and that the government has blown the events out of proportion and has treated the participants unjustly. Some supporters have described the rioters as political prisoners. His critics say that the attack was the culmination of a plan to overturn the election by any means, that the president knew the claims were false, that he had directed the crowd to the Capitol, and that his failure to stop the attack for hours was intentional.

The historians of the future will weigh these accounts. For now it is enough to say that the events of January 6 stand as the only occasion in American history on which a president tried, by a variety of means, to prevent the peaceful transfer of power to his successor. The Senate did not convict him. The courts, in the end, did not try him. And the voters, in 2024, returned him to the White House.

Chapter 18
The Defendant

Four Indictments

Between March and August of 2023, Donald Trump became the first former president in American history to be indicted, and then the first to be indicted four times. The cases were brought by three different prosecutors in three jurisdictions, on different theories, and they ended in very different ways. This chapter follows them in the order in which the charges were filed, and adds the civil cases that ran alongside, because in the public mind, and in Trump's, they belong together.

Trump's response to all of them was consistent. He called them a witch hunt, election interference, and the weaponization of the justice system. He argued that the prosecutors, who were Democrats in most cases, were pursuing him in order to prevent his return to office. His supporters agreed, and each indictment produced a burst of small-dollar fundraising. His critics said that the number of indictments was a function of the number of alleged crimes.

The Hush Money Case

The first charges came from Manhattan, from District Attorney Alvin Bragg. On March 30, 2023, a grand jury voted to indict Trump, and on April 4, he was arraigned in a courtroom in lower Manhattan on thirty-four felony counts of falsifying business records in the first degree. The charges arose from the payments made in 2016 to Stormy Daniels through Michael Cohen, described in Chapter Ten, and the way in which Trump's company had recorded the reimbursement to Cohen as legal expenses under a retainer agreement that did not exist. Under New York law, falsifying business records is a misdemeanor, but becomes a felony if it was done with the intent to commit or conceal another crime. The prosecution's theory was that the other crime was an unlawful conspiracy to promote Trump's election by illegal means, including violations of election law.

The case was widely criticized by legal commentators, including some who disliked Trump, as legally novel and, compared with the other cases, minor. It went to trial before Judge Juan Merchan in April 2024, and it lasted about six weeks. The prosecution's central witness was Cohen, who told the jury that Trump had directed the payments and knew of the false records. David Pecker of the National Enquirer testified about the catch-and-kill arrangement. Daniels testified about the encounter she said she had had with Trump. The defense argued that Cohen was a liar with a grudge, that Trump had not been involved in the details of the accounting, and that the payments were to protect his family and not his campaign. Trump did not testify.

On May 30, 2024, the jury deliberated for about twelve hours over two days, and found Trump guilty on all thirty-four counts. He became the first former president convicted of a crime. Merchan postponed the sentencing several times. Trump was elected in November while the sentencing was pending, and on January 10, 2025, ten days before his inauguration, Merchan sentenced him to an unconditional discharge, meaning that there was no jail time, no fine and no probation, but that the conviction would stand. The judge said that the only lawful sentence that would not intrude on the legal protections of the presidency-elect was an unconditional discharge. Trump has appealed, seeking to have the conviction overturned, and the appeals were still pending at the time of this writing; in August 2026, a federal court again rejected his effort to move the case out of the state courts.

The Documents Case

The second indictment, from the special counsel Jack Smith in the Southern District of Florida in June 2023, concerned the classified documents that Trump had taken from the White House to Mar-a-Lago when his term ended. After the National Archives asked for the return of presidential records, Trump returned fifteen boxes in January 2022, some of which contained classified material, and the government issued a subpoena in May for the rest. His lawyers returned some more documents and certified that a diligent search had been made. In August 2022, FBI agents executed a search warrant at Mar-a-Lago and recovered more than a hundred additional classified documents, some of them stored in a bathroom and a ballroom.

The indictment charged Trump with thirty-one counts of willful retention of national defense information, and additional counts of obstruction and false statements, relating to allegations that he had asked his lawyers to conceal boxes, and that he had shown a classified military plan to visitors at his golf club in Bedminster. It also charged two employees, Walt Nauta and Carlos De Oliveira. The most striking piece of evidence was an audio recording of Trump in 2021, in which he said of a document that it was highly confidential and secret, and that as president he could have declassified it, but that now he could not.

Trump argued that he had the authority under the Presidential Records Act to keep the documents and that he had declassified them by thinking about it. The case was assigned to Judge Aileen Cannon, whom Trump had appointed. She delayed the case for months, made a series of rulings favorable to the defense, and in July 2024 dismissed the case, holding that Smith's appointment as special counsel had been unlawful because Congress had not authorized it. Smith appealed, but after the election he dropped the appeal against Trump. The case against Nauta and De Oliveira was also dismissed.

The Georgia Case

In August 2023 a grand jury in Fulton County, Georgia, indicted Trump and eighteen others under the state's racketeering law, based on the effort to overturn the result in that state. The defendants included Giuliani, Meadows, Eastman, Powell, Ellis and others. The indictment alleged a criminal enterprise that included the phone call to Raffensperger, the assembly of slates of false electors, and pressure on state officials. Four of the defendants, including Powell and Ellis, pleaded guilty to reduced charges. In January 2024 the district attorney, Fani Willis, was accused of an inappropriate relationship with a prosecutor she had hired, Nathan Wade, and in December 2024 the Georgia Court of Appeals ruled that she should be disqualified. The case stalled, and in November 2025, after a successor prosecutor took it over, it was dismissed.

The Civil Cases

The civil litigation produced some of the most substantial financial judgments, and they have reached different outcomes.

In New York, Attorney General Letitia James sued Trump, his sons, and the Trump Organization in 2022, alleging that for a decade they had inflated the value of assets on financial statements provided to banks and insurers, in order to obtain better loan terms. In September 2023, Judge Arthur Engoron found before trial that the defendants were liable for fraud, and after a bench trial he ordered them, in February 2024, to pay about three hundred and fifty-five million dollars in disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, with interest, bringing the total to about four hundred and fifty-four million dollars, and barred Trump from serving as an officer of a New York company for three years. Among the findings was that Trump's financial statements had valued Mar-a-Lago and other properties at many times what the court found supportable. An appeals court in August 2025 threw out the monetary penalty as excessive, while leaving in place the finding of liability, and the matter went on to New York's highest court. The state, and Trump, each appealed parts of the ruling.

In the cases brought by the writer E. Jean Carroll, two federal juries found Trump liable. In May 2023 a Manhattan jury found that he had sexually abused Carroll in a department store dressing room in the 1990s, and that he had defamed her by calling her a liar, awarding her five million dollars. In January 2024, a second jury, in a separate trial about statements Trump made after the first, awarded her eighty-three point three million dollars for defamation. Trump denied the allegation and attacked Carroll repeatedly. Courts of appeals affirmed both verdicts. In June 2026, the Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal of the first verdict, and in August, it refused to reconsider. Trump's petition against the larger judgment was pending at the time of writing.

The Immunity Ruling and the Pattern

Taken together, the cases followed a sequence. In the New York criminal case, Trump was convicted, but suffered no punishment. In the two federal criminal cases, the prosecutions were derailed by a combination of judicial delay, the Supreme Court's decision on immunity, and the election result. In Georgia, the case collapsed under the weight of the prosecutor's own conduct. In the civil cases, he lost three verdicts and was ordered to pay very large sums, but has succeeded in postponing or reducing the largest ones.

To Trump's supporters this outcome vindicates his claim that the cases were political. They point out that the prosecutors were elected Democrats or, in Smith's case, appointed by one; that the New York case rested on a novel legal theory; that the civil fraud case involved no complaining victim, since the banks had been repaid; and that the judges in some cases showed hostility toward him. To his critics, the outcome shows the difficulty of holding a powerful person to account. A defendant with resources, they say, can use every procedural tool to delay, and a defendant who wins an election can render prosecution moot. Neither the timeline nor the record supports the view that he was innocent of the conduct charged, they say; it supports only the conclusion that the system could not reach him in time.

Whichever view one takes, the cases established that Trump is a convicted felon, a man found liable for sexual abuse and for fraud, and a president who twice faced the possibility of trial for acts committed in office. They did not prevent him from being elected. He has said that he will use his power to prosecute those who prosecuted him. That story continues in the chapters that follow.

Chapter 19
The Courts and the Constitution

A Litigant President

Trump has been in more courtrooms than any other American president. As a businessman he was involved in thousands of legal actions, as plaintiff and defendant; by one count, made by USA Today in 2016, he and his companies had been parties in about three and a half thousand lawsuits over three decades. As a politician, his cases have reached the highest court in the land on issues that touch the foundations of the constitutional system: the reach of presidential power, the meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment, the boundaries of executive immunity and the ability of Congress to limit the executive. This chapter looks at those cases and at the way the courts, and the Supreme Court in particular, have responded to a president who has tested their limits.

The Judges

The Supreme Court that Trump left behind in 2021 was not the one he inherited. Three of its nine members, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, are his appointees, and with Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito and Chief Justice John Roberts they form a majority that most observers describe as conservative. The lower courts also moved to the right, as he appointed more than two hundred federal judges, many of them selected from a list prepared by the Federalist Society and its executive vice president, Leonard Leo, and by the White House counsel Donald McGahn.

Trump has thus been a maker of courts. He has also been their critic. When federal judges have ruled against him, including judges he appointed, he has attacked them by name, calling some of them radical left lunatics or worse. In the second term, the White House and his allies have called for the impeachment of judges who have ruled against him. In March 2025, when a federal judge in Washington, James Boasberg, ordered the government to turn around planes carrying Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador, Trump called for his impeachment, and Chief Justice Roberts issued a rare statement saying that impeachment is not an appropriate response to disagreement about a judicial decision.

Trump v. Hawaii

The first major Supreme Court test of his presidency concerned the travel ban, the order to bar entry to citizens of several Muslim-majority countries. After two versions had been blocked in the lower courts, the third, which was issued in September 2017 and included North Korea and some Venezuelan officials, reached the Supreme Court. In June 2018, in Trump v. Hawaii, the Court upheld it, five to four, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts. He wrote that the president had broad authority under federal immigration law to restrict entry and that the ban was facially neutral toward religion. The opinion, which the dissenters called a repetition of the Court's mistake in upholding the internment of Japanese Americans in Korematsu v. United States, also went out of its way to say that Korematsu was wrongly decided.

The Colorado Ballot Case

In December 2023, the Colorado Supreme Court ruled that Trump was disqualified from the state's Republican primary ballot under Section Three of the Fourteenth Amendment, which bars from office anyone who took an oath to support the Constitution and later engaged in insurrection. The provision, adopted after the Civil War to keep former Confederates out of government, had rarely been used. The Colorado court found, after a trial, that Trump had engaged in insurrection on January 6.

The United States Supreme Court reversed unanimously in March 2024, in Trump v. Anderson. All nine justices agreed that states may not enforce Section Three against candidates for federal office, and that only Congress can do that. Five justices went further, saying that Congress alone could enforce the section through legislation. The three liberal justices concurred only in the judgment, saying that the majority had gone further than necessary. The Court did not decide whether Trump had engaged in insurrection.

Trump v. United States

The most significant decision, described in Chapter Seventeen, was the immunity ruling of July 1, 2024. By six to three, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts, the Court held that the president is entitled to absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for the exercise of his core constitutional powers, presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts. It added that evidence of official acts may not be used to prove the character of unofficial acts. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, in dissent, wrote that the decision made a mockery of the principle that no man is above the law, and warned that the president would be a king above the law. Chief Justice Roberts, in the opinion for the majority, said that the dissent's fears were overwrought.

The decision had immediate consequences: it delayed the election interference case beyond the election, and it required the New York courts to consider whether evidence used in the hush money trial should have been excluded. It also established a rule that was not contained in the Constitution's text, and whose defenders say that it was necessary to protect the presidency from harassment. Its critics say that it will be remembered as one of the Court's most consequential errors.

Emergency Docket

In the second term, the balance of power between the executive and the judiciary has been worked out largely through what is called the emergency docket, in which the Supreme Court decides applications for stays of lower court orders on an expedited basis without full briefing or argument. The administration made frequent use of it in 2025. In many cases, the Court granted the administration's requests: it allowed the government to end certain grants, to remove officials from independent agencies, to proceed with cuts to the federal workforce, and to end protections for some immigrants. In Trump v. CASA, in June 2025, the Court held that lower federal courts lack the power to issue universal injunctions, though it left open other means for broad relief.

There were exceptions. The Court ruled that the government must facilitate the return of a man who had been wrongly deported to El Salvador, and that migrants must be given notice and a chance to challenge their removal under the Alien Enemies Act. In the tariff case, Learning Resources v. Trump, described in Chapter Twenty-three, a majority that included three of the president's appointees ruled that the emergency statute on which he relied did not authorize the tariffs. In the summer of 2026, according to reporting, it rejected his attempt to remove a member of the Federal Reserve Board, Lisa Cook, on the ground that the Fed occupies a special position.

The Court's approach has been called pragmatic by some, and a betrayal of its role as a check by others. What is clear is that the justices have been willing to give the president broad power over the internal workings of the executive branch, and, as of the time of writing, less willing to endorse his claim to power over matters that the Constitution assigns to Congress, such as taxing and spending.

The Unitary Executive

Underlying many of these cases is a legal theory known as the unitary executive: the idea that the Constitution vests all executive power in the president, and that he must therefore be able to control and remove all officials who exercise it. The theory has been developed by conservative lawyers over four decades, and it is the intellectual foundation of the administration's efforts to bring independent agencies, such as the Federal Trade Commission and the National Labor Relations Board, under his control. The Court has accepted the theory in large part, though in the case of the Federal Reserve it has indicated that there may be limits.

Advocates say that the theory simply describes the text of Article Two, and that it restores accountability by making the president responsible for the actions of the executive. Critics say that it has no basis in the original understanding, and that it enables a president to remove any check on his power. The debate is scholarly in form, and the stakes are immense.

Contempt and Compliance

The most delicate question about the courts and this president is whether he will obey them. The record here is mixed. In the first term, Trump complied with adverse decisions, even those that he disliked, and did not defy the Supreme Court. In the second term, by contrast, judges in several cases have found that the administration has failed to comply with their orders, in matters relating to deportations, to the freezing of funds and to the deployment of troops. Some judges, including Boasberg, have initiated contempt proceedings. The administration's response has been to appeal, to slow-walk, and to attack, but it has not openly announced that it will disobey the Supreme Court. Vice President Vance has said that judges are not allowed to control the executive's legitimate power. Trump has said that he would obey the Court's rulings.

The distinction between defiance and delay is important, and it is one that the country will have to watch. As of the writing of this chapter, no president in American history has openly defied a final order of the Supreme Court. The tariff decision, in which the president complied by ending the tariffs, though he then found other ways to impose them, is an example of the pattern: compliance in form, and resistance in substance.

Chapter 20
The Republican Party Remade

A Hostile Takeover

In 2015, the Republican Party was, in the view of most of its leaders, a coalition of three elements: business conservatives who wanted low taxes and light regulation, social conservatives who wanted restrictions on abortion and the defense of religious liberty, and national security conservatives who wanted a strong military and an assertive American role in the world. Its presidential candidates, from Ronald Reagan through George W. Bush to Mitt Romney, had supported free trade, immigration reform of one kind or another, and the alliance system built after 1945. Trump ran against nearly all of it.

His victory in the primaries was, by any measure, a hostile takeover. He defeated sixteen rivals, many of whom had greater experience and more support from the party's donors and institutions. In the general election he won with the votes of the party's rank and file and of many voters who had not previously been Republicans. Within a few years, he had reshaped its platform, its personnel and its identity. By 2024, the party's leaders, who had once regarded him as a threat, competed to declare their loyalty to him.

The Resistance of the Establishment

It was not an easy transition. In 2016, a group of prominent Republican foreign policy officials signed letters declaring that Trump was unfit for office. Some of the party's most senior figures, including the last two Republican presidents and Mitt Romney, the 2012 nominee, declined to support him. In the Senate, a small number of Republicans, including John McCain, Jeff Flake, Bob Corker and Mitt Romney, criticized him at various points. McCain cast the vote that killed the repeal of the Affordable Care Act. Flake and Corker retired, saying that they could not win a primary while opposing him.

The 2018 midterm elections were a rebuke, in the sense that Democrats won forty seats and control of the House, the largest gain since Watergate. But in the same election, Republicans gained seats in the Senate, and Trump's endorsement became the most valuable asset in a Republican primary. The lesson, which his critics inside the party drew and acted upon by leaving Congress, was that Republican primary voters were with him.

After January 6

The critical test of his hold on the party came after the attack on the Capitol. In the days that followed, some prominent Republicans said that Trump had crossed a line. Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell said that he bore moral responsibility. Seven Republican senators voted to convict him in the second impeachment trial, and ten House Republicans voted to impeach. But within weeks, it became clear that his standing among the party's voters was intact. In May 2021, Representative Liz Cheney, the third-ranking Republican in the House and the daughter of a former vice president, was removed from her leadership post for saying that the election had not been stolen. In August 2022, she lost her primary in Wyoming to a Trump-backed challenger, Harriet Hageman, by more than thirty points. Of the ten House Republicans who voted to impeach, only two were in office in 2025. Some had retired and others lost primaries.

Republicans on the January 6 committee, Cheney and Adam Kinzinger, were both censured by the Republican National Committee in February 2022, in a resolution that described what they were investigating as legitimate political discourse. Kevin McCarthy, who had said on the floor of the House that Trump bore responsibility for the attack, flew to Mar-a-Lago weeks afterwards to make peace. The partial recovery from the events of January 6 is one of the more striking episodes in modern politics.

The Elections of 2022 and 2024

The party's fortunes without Trump were mixed. In the 2022 midterms, the candidates he endorsed in many primaries, some of whom had embraced the false claims about the 2020 election, lost in the general election in states such as Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and New Hampshire. Republicans won the House by a slim margin but failed to take the Senate, and many in the party blamed him. Ron DeSantis's landslide reelection in Florida briefly made him the party's presumed future.

Then came the indictments. By turning each one into a test of loyalty, and by making the claim that he was being persecuted on behalf of his supporters, Trump consolidated the party behind him. By the beginning of 2024 he had a lead in the polls of more than thirty points over DeSantis, and a Republican primary electorate that told pollsters that it did not believe that any of the charges were serious. He won the nomination without a debate, and, in November, the presidency. The party won the Senate, with a majority of fifty-three, and retained control of the House.

The Changing Coalition

What is more remarkable than the party's loyalty is the change in its electorate. The Republican Party that Trump inherited was strongest among affluent, college-educated voters. The party that he leaves, if he leaves, is strongest among working-class voters, who, particularly outside the big cities, have moved toward it in every election since 2012. In 2016, the shift among white voters without college degrees was the decisive factor in the Rust Belt. In 2020 and 2024, the party made gains among Hispanic voters, particularly men, and among some Black men and young men, though the numbers remain small. The wealthiest suburbs have moved in the other direction, toward the Democrats. Since 2016, the two parties have, to a degree, traded places in the class structure of American politics.

The change also affected the party's policies. The Trump Republicans are, in many respects, more populist than their predecessors. They are hostile to free trade agreements and to the entitlement cuts that were once a Republican staple, more skeptical of foreign intervention and of Ukraine, more concerned with immigration, more hostile to large technology companies and to universities, and more willing to use the power of government against their perceived opponents. In other respects, they resemble the earlier party: they favor tax cuts, deregulation, restrictions on abortion and the appointment of conservative judges.

MAGA Inc.

The movement that Trump created is known by the slogan of his campaigns, Make America Great Again, and by the red baseball cap that became its emblem. It is not a formal organization, though it has institutions: the Heritage Foundation, which published Project 2025, a lengthy set of proposals for a second Trump administration, in 2023 and 2024 (Trump said during the campaign that he knew nothing about it and disagreed with some of it, but many of its authors held positions in his administration, and many of its proposals have been carried out); Turning Point USA, the youth organization founded by Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated at a university event in Utah in September 2025, an event that shook the movement and led to an outpouring of grief; the network of podcasters, streamers and social media influencers who reach audiences that traditional media do not; and the super PAC that gathered money for his campaigns and legal fees.

Its leaders in Congress include Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who was elected to the office in October 2023 and who has rarely defied him, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, who succeeded McConnell in January 2025. Vice President Vance is widely seen as his most likely heir. Whether the movement will survive Trump is a question that many Republicans are already asking. The party's history suggests that movements built around a single charismatic figure often fade with his departure, but, as some analysts point out, the conditions that gave rise to him, the resentment of elites and the decline of trust in institutions, remain.

Fissures

Signs of strain have appeared in the second term. The war with Iran has divided the movement. Some of Trump's closest allies in conservative media, who supported his promises of no new wars, have criticized the decision to go to war, and some of his supporters have described the conflict as a betrayal of his promise to end endless wars. The tariffs, and the rise of inflation, have created dissent among the Republican members of Congress from farm states and from export industries. The handling of the Epstein files was a source of anger among his most devoted followers. The falling out with Elon Musk in 2025 demonstrated that even the most powerful supporters could not be sure of his favor.

None of these has yet cost him his hold on the party. Polls consistently show that roughly eight in ten Republicans approve of his performance, even as his approval among the public as a whole has fallen to the mid-thirties. That is the paradox at the center of his political position. He holds one of the most complete grips on a major party in American history, and he leads that party toward an election in which, according to the polls, it may lose control of the House. The result of that election will be the first test of whether the grip is enough.

Chapter 21
The Comeback

Announcing From Exile

Donald Trump announced his candidacy for a third consecutive Republican nomination on November 15, 2022, one week after midterm elections that had gone badly for the party. Candidates he had endorsed lost several of the most closely watched races, and the red wave that had been predicted did not arrive. Many Republicans blamed him, and for a time it seemed that his influence was fading. Some in the party and in conservative media, including Rupert Murdoch's newspapers, looked to Florida Governor Ron DeSantis as the future.

Trump's response was to drive on. He had the advantage of near-universal name recognition, a loyal base, and a fundraising machine. He also had the advantage, unexpected but crucial, of the indictments. Each one, in the months that followed, provoked a rally around him. Republican rivals who might have criticized his conduct found themselves defending his right to a fair trial, and Trump's poll numbers among Republicans rose after each indictment. He skipped every primary debate. He won the Iowa caucuses in January 2024 by thirty points, the largest margin in the history of the contested caucus. DeSantis dropped out two days later. Nikki Haley, the former governor of South Carolina and his ambassador to the United Nations, lasted until March, after winning only Vermont and the District of Columbia. By March 12 Trump had clinched the nomination.

Biden and the Debate

The Democratic nominee seemed, until the end of June, to be President Joe Biden. But Biden, at eighty-one, was widely regarded as too old for the job, and polls consistently showed that most Americans, including most Democrats, doubted his capacity for a second term. On June 27, in Atlanta, in the first debate of the general election, held early at Biden's request, the president appeared confused, spoke haltingly and lost his train of thought. At one point he ended an answer on health care by saying that we finally beat Medicare. Trump, for his part, made a number of false statements that were noted by fact-checkers, but that were overshadowed by the coverage of Biden's performance.

Within days, prominent Democrats were calling on Biden to withdraw. He resisted for three weeks. On July 21, he announced on social media that he would not seek reelection and endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris. She quickly consolidated the party's support and was nominated at the Democratic convention in Chicago in August. Her selection of Governor Tim Walz of Minnesota as running mate, and a new energy among Democrats, produced a brief surge in the polls.

Butler

Two weeks before Biden's withdrawal, an event took place that altered the character of the race. On July 13, 2024, at a rally at the Butler Farm Show grounds in Butler, Pennsylvania, a twenty-year-old man named Thomas Matthew Crooks climbed onto the roof of a nearby building and fired eight shots at the former president from about a hundred and thirty yards away. One bullet grazed Trump's right ear. Trump ducked, was tackled by Secret Service agents, and then, bleeding, rose with his fist in the air and shouted Fight, fight, fight. A photograph of the moment by Evan Vucci of the Associated Press, showing Trump with blood on his face and the American flag behind him, became an emblem of the campaign.

Corey Comperatore, a fifty-year-old former fire chief who was attending the rally, was shot and killed, and two other spectators were badly wounded. Crooks was shot and killed by a Secret Service counter-sniper. The investigations that followed, by Congress and by an independent panel, found that the Secret Service had made serious errors in planning and communication, including its failure to secure the roof from which Crooks fired, despite knowing that it was a vulnerability. The director, Kimberly Cheatle, resigned. The FBI did not find a clear motive.

In September a second attempt was made on Trump's life at his golf course in West Palm Beach, Florida, when a man named Ryan Routh was found with a rifle in the bushes near the course. He was convicted of attempted assassination in 2025. Trump's supporters saw providential meaning in his escape. Trump himself said that he was saved by God.

The Campaign

The Trump campaign of 2024 was disciplined in a way that his earlier campaigns had not been. It was run by Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita, professionals who had won the confidence of the candidate and his family, and its message was focused on two issues: inflation, which had risen sharply during the Biden years and left prices for groceries, housing and cars much higher than in 2020, and immigration, which had reached record levels at the southern border. Trump said that he would carry out the largest deportation operation in American history, would impose tariffs of ten to twenty percent on all imports and sixty percent or more on imports from China, and would cut taxes. He also promised to end the war in Ukraine within a day, a boast that he later described as hyperbole.

His rhetoric grew harsher. He said that immigrants were poisoning the blood of the country. He claimed at a September debate that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating the cats and dogs of residents, a claim that local authorities said had no evidence behind it. He called his political enemies the enemy within and said that they should be dealt with by the National Guard or, if necessary, the military. At a rally at Madison Square Garden in the last week of the campaign, a comedian who spoke before him called Puerto Rico a floating island of garbage, which the campaign distanced itself from, and Biden characterized Trump's supporters in a phrase that his own aides then had to walk back.

He also received the support of the world's richest man. Elon Musk, the head of Tesla and SpaceX and the owner of the social network X, endorsed Trump after the assassination attempt and spent about two hundred and fifty million dollars through a political action committee that he created. He campaigned with Trump in Pennsylvania and offered a million dollars a day to registered voters in swing states who signed a petition, a scheme that prosecutors examined. In return, Trump said, Musk would work on cutting government spending.

Harris and the Debate

Kamala Harris, at fifty-nine, had never been an especially popular vice president, but as the nominee she raised the Democrats' hopes. In the one debate, on September 10 in Philadelphia, she was widely judged to have done better, and Trump was seen as having been pushed onto the defensive on his own record. Why He Won

Explanations for the outcome abound, and they are not mutually exclusive. The most straightforward is that the incumbent party was punished for high inflation, as incumbent parties were around the world in 2024. A second is that voters were more concerned about immigration than had been understood. A third is that Biden's late withdrawal, at age eighty-one, left Harris with too little time to define herself. A fourth is that Trump's message, whatever its extravagances, connected with voters who felt that the system did not work for them. A fifth is that the media environment, in which many people got their news from podcasts and social media, favored a candidate who dominated attention, and that Trump's appearance on shows like Joe Rogan's, which drew tens of millions of viewers, reached audiences the Harris campaign did not.

The fact that Trump won despite a felony conviction, two impeachments, and the events of January 6, was held by his supporters to be a verdict of the voters on these matters. His critics took a different view. They said that voters had been more concerned with the price of eggs than with the fate of constitutional norms, and that a majority had not endorsed the conduct in question; they had simply, in the end, decided that other things mattered more. It was a plausible reading, and it was the beginning of the second term.

By the end of 2025 the outlines of the second term were clear.
