Eighty

On June 14, 2026, Donald Trump turned eighty. He is the oldest person ever inaugurated as president, having taken the oath for the second time at seventy-eight, and at eighty he is within two years of the age at which Joe Biden left office. That fact is inescapable in any assessment of his second term, and it has been the subject of a good deal of speculation, some of it informed, some of it partisan. This chapter tries to separate what is known from what is asserted.

The subject has to be treated with care. A president's health is a matter of legitimate public concern, because the ability of a president to discharge the duties of the office is a matter of national importance. But it is also an area in which observers, viewing a public figure from a distance, are prone to draw conclusions that they cannot support. The author is not a physician, and this chapter will offer none.

What Is on the Record

The public record of Trump's health consists of the statements of his physicians, medical summaries released by the White House, and events that have been observed. As a candidate in 2016, he released a letter from his doctor, Harold Bornstein, which said that he would be the healthiest individual ever elected to the presidency. Bornstein later said that Trump had dictated the letter. In 2018 the White House physician, Ronny Jackson, gave a briefing in which he said that Trump had excellent cognitive function, and that if Trump had had a healthier diet over the past twenty years he might live to be two hundred. Trump's cholesterol, weight and use of medication have been documented in periodic reports. His weight at the 2018 examination was recorded at two hundred and thirty-nine pounds. In 2020, he was hospitalized with COVID-19 at Walter Reed, in an episode in which his physicians offered limited information, and in which officials at the time were less than forthcoming about his condition.

In the second term, the White House has released periodic summaries of examinations. In July 2025, the White House announced that the president had been diagnosed with chronic venous insufficiency, a common condition in older adults in which the veins in the legs do not return blood to the heart efficiently, causing swelling. The White House physician said that the condition was benign and not serious, and that tests had found no sign of deep vein thrombosis or arterial disease. Aides also said that the bruising on Trump's hands, which had been visible for months, was the result of frequent handshakes and of aspirin that he takes as part of a cardiovascular regimen. In October 2025, he visited Walter Reed for what the White House described as a routine physical, including what it said was advanced imaging, and subsequent summaries described his health as excellent. The president has said that he takes a test of cognitive function periodically and that he did well on it, and he has made a point of challenging opponents to do the same.

The Public Debate

The subject of Trump's age gained particular force after the debate in June 2024 in which President Biden's performance led to his withdrawal from the race. Before it, Trump and his allies had been prominent in questioning Biden's capacity, and the argument that a president's age matters was widely made. It became difficult, afterward, for Republicans to make the case, and for Democrats to avoid the observation that Trump, at seventy-eight, was only a few years younger than Biden had been at the start of his term.

Since the beginning of the second term, some commentators have pointed to moments in which the president appeared to fall asleep at public events, to his occasional verbal slips, and to what they see as a pattern of confusion or incoherence in his speeches. His aides reply that he works long days, that he is far more energetic than his critics recognize, and that clips of his lapses are selectively edited. Neither view can be tested by outsiders. Polls show that a large share of Americans, including some Republicans, believe that he is too old for the job, though the proportion is smaller than the proportion who said the same of Biden in 2024.

The Constitutional Mechanisms

The Constitution provides two mechanisms for dealing with a president who cannot discharge his duties. The first is the Twenty-fifth Amendment, ratified in 1967, which allows the vice president and a majority of the cabinet to declare the president unable to serve, and the president to contest their decision, in which case Congress decides by a two-thirds vote. It has never been used to remove a president against his will. The second is impeachment. Neither is likely to be invoked over a matter of age, and both would require political consensus that does not exist.

The alternative is the voluntary and orderly management of succession, in which the president, the vice president and the party plan for the moment when he can no longer serve. In the second term, that role has been accepted by JD Vance, who is forty-two, and who has been a loyal deputy. Whether the country will treat him as an heir apparent is a question the midterms may answer.

The Third Term

There is a related subject. The Twenty-second Amendment provides that no person shall be elected to the office of President more than twice. Trump, who was elected in 2016 and 2024, is therefore ineligible to be elected again. He has nonetheless toyed with the subject. He has said on several occasions that he would like to serve a third term, has joked about it, and has allowed his supporters to sell hats with the slogan Trump 2028. In October 2025, asked about it directly, he said that he was not allowed to run and that it was too bad. Some of his advisers, including Steve Bannon, have suggested that there is a way. Most constitutional scholars say that there is not.

The debate shows a truth about his position. He is the leader of a movement in which the bond between the man and his followers is so strong that many have difficulty imagining the movement without him. The most important test of the durability of American political institutions in the coming years may be whether, on January 20, 2029, power passes to a successor as the Constitution requires.

A Portrait at Eighty

Trump at eighty is, in many respects, the man that he has been for fifty years: energetic, combative, attentive to his image, uninterested in self-reflection, preoccupied with what is said about him. He remains a compulsive user of television and social media, often posting late at night. His approval rating is near the lowest of his career, and the war that he began in February has become an unwelcome burden on the country. He is, by the accounts of his critics, unwilling to consider the possibility that the strategy he pursued for a lifetime might no longer work, and by the accounts of his allies, as determined as he has ever been.

If there is a pattern in his conduct, it is that he has always responded to adversity by escalating, and that he has, so far, survived. Whether that will continue is a question on which the record offers no guidance, because no president has faced these circumstances at this age, and because it is the nature of a life like his to defy predictions. It is the reason that this biography ends, as it must, without a conclusion.

Chapter 26
The Case for the Defense

Why This Chapter

A biography that says only what critics say is a brief, not a book. Trump has been elected president twice, and won the votes of more than seventy-seven million Americans in 2024. Whatever else one thinks, a movement of that size cannot be explained by fraud or ignorance. This chapter presents the argument that his supporters and defenders make, in their strongest form, and, where the record permits, notes what critics say in reply. It is the case others would make, not the author's own conclusion.

The Outsider Who Kept Faith

The heart of the case is that Trump is the one political figure in a generation who was willing to say what a large segment of the public believed and no one in power would say. For decades, his defenders argue, both parties governed for the benefit of a class of professionals, financiers and officials who prospered from globalization while manufacturing towns emptied and wages stagnated. Republican leaders talked about the working class and delivered tax cuts for donors and wars overseas. Democratic leaders talked about fairness and delivered bailouts for banks. Trump, in this account, said what the voters were thinking about trade, immigration, endless wars and the arrogance of elites, and he was punished for it by the entire establishment, including the press, the intelligence agencies, the universities and the courts.

His supporters point to the results in the first term as a vindication of the claim that he keeps his promises. He cut taxes and regulation. He appointed hundreds of judges and three Supreme Court justices who, in Dobbs, overturned Roe v. Wade, the decision that the pro-life movement had opposed for almost half a century. He moved the American embassy to Jerusalem. He withdrew from an Iran deal that he considered dangerous. He brokered the Abraham Accords, the first normalization agreements between Israel and Arab states in a quarter century. He confronted China's trade practices, a position that, once considered radical, is now held by much of both parties. He replaced NAFTA. He signed the First Step Act, criminal justice reform that reduced sentences for thousands of federal prisoners, with support from both parties. He rebuilt part of the military, and, unlike his predecessors, started no new war in four years.

The Economy

Supporters point to the economy before the pandemic. In 2019 unemployment reached fifty-year lows, wages for the lowest-paid workers rose faster than those of the highest, and household income reached record levels. Trump's defenders credit the tax cuts and deregulation, and argue that the pattern demonstrated that a president who was hostile to the regulatory state could unleash growth. They contrast this with the inflation of the early 1980s and again of 2021 to 2023, when prices for groceries, rent, gasoline and cars rose sharply. Many voters, they say, remembered the Trump years as a time when they could afford things, and the 2024 election was a verdict on that memory.

They also credit him with Operation Warp Speed, the government program that helped produce effective vaccines within a year, a feat that many experts had thought impossible, and which almost certainly saved lives.

The Border

Border enforcement is the cause that first made Trump a national figure. His supporters say that the numbers in the Biden years, with millions of illegal crossings, showed that the system had been overwhelmed, and that the failure to control it imposed real costs on cities and on the workers who competed with the newcomers. They argue that it was Trump's willingness to be harsh that brought the numbers down: illegal crossings in 2025 fell to a level not seen in half a century. They say that it is not extreme to enforce the laws that Congress has passed and to expect that people who enter illegally will be removed.

The Prosecutions and the Press

The most emotional part of the defense concerns the legal cases. Trump's supporters say that the prosecutions were unprecedented, unfair, and political. They say that the Manhattan case rested on a novel legal theory, turning a misdemeanor for which the statute of limitations had run into a felony by borrowing an uncharged federal crime, and that many legal scholars, including some who despised Trump, thought it weak. They note that the Mar-a-Lago documents case had been brought against a former president by the administration of his opponent, while the treatment of documents found in the possession of Joe Biden was different. They note that the New York civil fraud case was brought by an attorney general who had campaigned on a promise to go after Trump, and that it involved no victim who claimed to have lost money, since the banks had been repaid with interest; an appeals court threw out the half-billion dollar penalty as excessive. They cite the fact that the Georgia case collapsed after the prosecutor's conduct became a scandal, and that the federal election case was stopped by the Supreme Court.

They also argue that the Russia investigation was itself an abuse of power. The record on this point is not merely partisan. The Justice Department's inspector general found serious errors and omissions in the surveillance applications relating to Carter Page. The special counsel Durham found that the FBI had opened its investigation on thin evidence, and that agents had been quick to credit the unverified Steele dossier, which had been financed by the Clinton campaign. In the view of Trump's supporters, three years of coverage of a collusion narrative that turned out to be unproven had helped to poison the country's politics, and was a scandal in its own right. They add that when the intelligence community and the press treated the story of Hunter Biden's laptop as probably Russian disinformation in 2020, and when dozens of former officials signed a letter to that effect, that the elites had shown their partiality.

The Media

Many of Trump's supporters believe that the press is not simply hostile but dishonest. They point to the rush of coverage of the Steele dossier, to media reports in 2020 that Russia had paid bounties for the killing of American troops in Afghanistan, which the intelligence community later said it could not confirm, and to the way that the president's remarks on Charlottesville were covered. The full sentence in which Trump said that neo-Nazis and white nationalists should be condemned totally, they say, was too often omitted. They argue that the press is dominated by people who share the politics of the Democratic Party, that their disdain is transparent, and that voters are right to distrust them. Trump's confrontational style, on this view, is not a flaw but a correction.

The Foreign Policy of Restraint and Strength

Supporters see a coherent foreign policy in his conduct. He pressed NATO allies to spend more on their own defense, and they have, in the last year raising their commitments to five percent of GDP. He questioned assumptions about American commitments abroad. He opened talks with North Korea. He did not, in the first term, leave American troops in new wars, and his order to kill the Iranian general Qassem Soleimani in January 2020 was, in the view of supporters, an example of decisive action that deterred Iran from broader attacks. In the second term, they argue, the strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025 and the capture of Maduro showed that America's adversaries could no longer assume that it would not act. They believe that a regime that had killed Americans for forty years and sought a bomb had to be confronted, and that the president had the courage to do it.

The Answer

The critics have answers to each of these arguments, and a fair account should state them. On the record of the first term, critics say that the credit for the economy belongs largely to the expansion that began under his predecessor, that the deficit rose sharply in good times, that manufacturing jobs did not return, and that the trade war hurt farmers and consumers. On the border, they note that crossings had fallen before he took office, that the surge in his first term was connected to policies such as family separation that horrified many of his own supporters, and that in the second term the enforcement has swept up people with no criminal record, and involved the deployment of the military in American cities.

On the legal cases, critics say that a jury of twelve New Yorkers unanimously convicted him on thirty-four counts on the evidence, that another jury found him liable for sexual abuse, that a judge found after a trial that he committed fraud, and that the delays which prevented the federal cases from being tried were the result of his own strategy and of a Supreme Court decision that invented a doctrine of immunity that the Constitution does not mention. They add that the law does not exempt a person from prosecution because he is a candidate.

On the election of 2020, they say, no defense is possible. Trump lost, was told that he had lost by his own officials, and refused to accept the result. Sixty courts, many with judges he had appointed, rejected the claims of fraud. There is no way to reconcile the events of January 6 with a commitment to the peaceful transfer of power that has been the foundation of American democracy since 1801.

On the tariffs, critics note that a Supreme Court that includes three of his own appointees held that the central legal basis was unlawful. On the Iran war, they say that the country has been dragged into a costly and open-ended conflict without the authorization of Congress. On the conduct of government, they point to the firing of inspectors general, the prosecutions of political opponents, and the use of pardons for allies as evidence of a president who has placed the machinery of the state at the service of his personal interests.

The debate between these two sets of arguments is, in the end, a debate about what a democracy requires of its leaders and what it owes to those who feel that it has failed them. Each side is convinced that the other has misunderstood the stakes. It is not the author's task to decide the argument for the reader. It is only to insist that both sides be heard, and that their claims be tested against what is documented.

Chapter 27
Assessment

What the Record Supports

The task of a final chapter in a critical biography is to say what has been established, what has not, and what remains open. It should do so without pretending that the answers are simpler than they are.

On character and honesty. The evidence that Trump makes false statements at an extraordinary rate is not in serious dispute. The Washington Post's count of more than thirty thousand false or misleading claims in the first term is one measure, and the pattern has, by most accounts, continued. The pattern predates politics. The overstated size of the penthouse, the inflated net worth given to Forbes, the fictitious spokesman named John Miller, the birther claim, the claims about the size of the inauguration crowd and the claims about the 2020 election form a single continuous thread. It is a legitimate question whether this is calculation, a form of salesmanship, or a deeper disregard for the distinction between true and false. The evidence supports the first two. About the third, the author cannot say.

On business. The image of Trump as a brilliant and self-made builder is not supported by the record. He began with substantial help from his father, benefited from public subsidies, and lost money in the casino business, needing a bailout from banks in 1990. He recovered by licensing his name, a business model that involved little risk to himself. At the same time, it would be wrong to say that he was merely a beneficiary. He had an instinct for publicity, for the value of a name, and for the way the press could be used, and he built a brand that endured. Whether he is as rich as he has said remains uncertain, since his finances are private and his tax returns show repeated losses.

On the law. Trump has been found liable by juries for sexual abuse and defamation, by a judge for civil fraud, and by a jury guilty on thirty-four felony counts of falsifying business records. The last of these is under appeal, and the fraud penalty was set aside as excessive, with the liability finding standing. He has also been the subject of prosecutions that were dismissed or derailed, and in the view of his defenders the two federal cases and the Georgia case would not have been brought against another person. The Supreme Court's decision on immunity in 2024 established that presidents cannot be prosecuted for official acts within their core powers, and left many questions open. The most defensible conclusion is that the record includes findings of wrongdoing by courts and juries, and also episodes in which prosecutors overreached or made errors, and that the system has not yet held the former president to account in the ways that many people expected.

On democracy. The events after the 2020 election are the most serious matter in the record. It is documented that Trump was told repeatedly by his own advisers that he had lost, that he pursued dozens of legal challenges that failed, that he pressed state officials and the vice president to change the result, and that he did not act for hours while the Capitol was under attack. Whether this amounted to a crime was, in the end, not decided by a court. That it violated the norms of American democracy is a conclusion that has been reached by many Republicans as well as Democrats. At the same time, the voters knew all of this and elected him again, and that too is a fact about democracy that any honest assessment must include.

On governing. The first term saw substantial policy change in taxes, regulation, the courts, trade and foreign policy, alongside chaos in the White House. The second term has seen an attempt at a much more sweeping transformation of the government: the dismantling of agencies, mass deportation, unilateral use of tariffs, military force against Venezuela and Iran, and confrontation with the courts and the press. Some of it has been reversed by the courts, notably in the tariff decision. Some of it, notably the war with Iran, has had consequences that are still unfolding. It is too early to judge the results. The president's approval rating, at about thirty-six percent in September 2026, suggests that the public is not satisfied with what it has seen.

Patterns

Reading the record as a whole, a few patterns stand out.

The first is a consistent method in the face of accusation: deny, attack, and declare victory, the method that Roy Cohn taught, and which he has applied from the housing discrimination case of 1973 to the indictments of 2023. It has often worked. It has also produced results that a more cautious person would have avoided.

The second is a talent for attention, and for turning bad publicity into an asset. From the tabloids of the 1980s, through The Apprentice, to the mug shot that became a campaign product, he has understood that being at the center of the story is a form of power.

The third is a habit of treating institutions as instruments. In business, the institutions were banks, lenders, and city governments, and he learned to make them serve his ends. In politics, the institutions are the courts, the Justice Department, Congress and the press, and he has treated them with the same expectation.

The fourth is the durability of the bond with his supporters. Whatever his failures, the loyalty of his base has survived scandals, indictments and defeats that would have ended other careers. Understanding why is the most important unanswered question in the study of his career. Part of the answer, no doubt, lies in what the critics have missed: in the sense of neglect, of disrespect, and of institutional failure that Trump gave voice to and that has not gone away.

What Remains Open

Several questions are unresolved as this book goes to press. Whether the Republicans will hold the House in November will determine whether the president faces investigations and, perhaps, impeachment for a third time. Whether the war in Iran will end or expand will shape the economy and his standing. The courts will decide the fate of the hush money conviction on appeal, the fraud judgment at the state's highest court, and the eighty-three million dollar Carroll verdict. The Constitution, as amended, bars a president from a third term, though Trump has occasionally teased the idea; if he does not run, the party will have to decide what it is without him.

Beyond these, there is the question that historians will ask. In the long arc of American history, will Donald Trump be seen as an aberration, a man who exploited a moment of disaffection and was then rejected, or as the founder of a new political order, whose methods and priorities will outlast him? The evidence of the 2024 election, of the power he retains over the Republican Party, and of the fact that the Democrats have had to define themselves in opposition to him, suggests that the answer may lie closer to the second than his opponents would like. But the evidence of 2026, of a president with a low approval rating who has been checked by the courts and challenged by the electorate, suggests that the limits of his power are also real.

A Last Word

It is a mistake to write of Trump as if he were unique in every respect. The tools he used, the manipulation of the press, the use of legal threats, the courting of resentment, and the personalization of political conflict, have precedents in American history, from Andrew Jackson to Richard Nixon to Joseph McCarthy. What is different is the combination of these tools with a talent for spectacle, at a time when the media environment rewards it, and at a moment when trust in institutions was at its lowest in living memory.

The story of Donald Trump is in many ways the story of the failure of those institutions to command the trust of the citizens they were meant to serve, and of the failure of the same institutions to hold a powerful and unconventional man to their standards. Both failures matter. The reader who leaves this book with a stronger sense of one and not the other has not read it carefully.

What remains is the reader's judgment. The documents are available. The court records, the tax returns, the transcripts and the reports are public, and this book has tried to point the way to them. Citizens in a democracy have the responsibility to read them, and to decide for themselves.
